The distribution of hydrogen in intergalactic space, as observed through absorption features in quasar spectra at ultraviolet wavelengths, provides a three-dimensional map of the universe's structure. Analyzing this distribution reveals how matter is clumped together on scales exceeding 10 megaparsecs, allowing researchers to directly infer the overall geometry of matter in the universe. Researchers used this approach to analyze data from the SDSS-MaNGA survey, discovering that the distribution of hydrogen clumps remains consistent with a flat and open universe, regardless of redshift levels up to 0.45. Interestingly, this flat-universe model contradicts findings from galaxy distributions at redshifts close to 0.45, which suggest a cosmology with a critical density and curvature. Researchers speculate that this discrepancy could be attributed to imperfect corrections for the effects of local galaxy structures on intergalactic hydrogen distributions.

The LANSCE's Beam Transfer Line experiment has demonstrated that an inhomogeneous magnetic field along the beam path induces an asymmetrical field that imparts energy rotations and leads to emittance transformations, an effect that cannot be eliminated by a quadrupole lens. This phenomenon, which can be mitigated to some extent, is not fully reversible in a multi-stage accelerator or transport system due to stochastic influences, resulting in losses of transverse emittance and potential disruptions to stable beams. Consequently, an emittance transformer, or "emittance cooker," emerges as a significant issue in modern beam diagnostics. Furthermore, our findings also reveal, through a study of the LANSCE's Beam Transfer Line experiment, that specific types of magnetic fields can serve as emittance transformers and that an emittance detector, which may be as simple as a single wall heater, can be employed to detect differences in transverse and longitudinal emittances.

This paper introduces a novel sliding sequential conditional variational autoencoder model for trajectory forecasting that can account for dynamic social contexts. Building upon the conventional trajectory forecasting task, our approach emphasizes the importance of future paths that can avoid collisions and maintain social interactions. To achieve this, we propose a sliding sequential Rethinking 2D-Group velocity model that varies over time. In contrast to fixed contextual models, our technique allows for capturing evolving social relationships. Furthermore, our approach represents the future trajectory as a combination of a mean path derived from the current trajectory and surrounding social context, and a stochastic variation representing uncertainty. By employing a sliding window, our method can capture both short-term trajectory details and long-term trend information. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed technique surpasses existing methods on standard datasets.

Over the past decade, researchers have applied information theory to artificial intelligence, including neural networks, to quantify computational complexity and measure tradeoffs in network design. To address these goals, several information-theoretic metrics have been developed, but they often focus on singular aspects of the learning process and lack comprehensive guidance for optimizing network performance. To bridge this gap, we introduce a suite of information-theoretic measures tailored to binary probabilistic neural networks and stochastic BMs. We apply these metrics to a standardbm dataset to explore their properties within high-dimensional BM landscapes, where parameters and data reside in discrete, probabilistic states. We examine relationships between these metrics to identify connections between sufficient statistics, data compression, network states, and mutual information. Our findings highlight the limitations of individual metrics and the need for a more holistic approach that considers multiple, interacting factors. Ultimately, we propose an information-theoretic objective function that balances these metrics for a more effective optimization of binary networks.

This study examines the potential effectiveness of hand gestures as communication tools between humans and swarms of robots. Our research method involved developing a machine learning model that can identify basic hand gestures in a real-world setting. We also evaluated the results when this motion recognition capability was integrated into a swarm of four quadcopters led by a human operator. To facilitate hand gesture recognition in a more energy-efficient manner, we employed a hierarchical architecture based on a global-local search strategy within a deep learning model. Our experiment involved testing the communication protocol in both controlled and real environments. Our findings reveal a good match between predicted and actual robot positions, with the majority of errors being under a degree in both settings. Furthermore, when this motion recognition protocol was utilized for guiding a swarm of robots, we observed that it was possible to steer the swarm with an average error rate of less than a degree. Our experiment also demonstrated that motion recognition performance remained stable even when the human operator or the robots were moved to different positions.

The study addresses the challenge of classifying blood cells into three main categories: WBC, RBC, and NBCD through the use of a multi-NN model. We utilize two individual neural networks, one for distinguishing between NB-CD and WBC, and another to differentiate between RBC and WBC. The two models' outputs are then combined using a merging strategy to distinguish between these two categories. Our proposed approach achieves an 89.7% accuracy in distinguishing between RBC and WBC, and a 95.3% accuracy in distinguishing between NB-CD and WBC. The integration of these two models results in a 98.4% accuracy in classifying an image as either RBC or WBC. We test the performance of our approach on a dataset of 1,000 blood cell images, with comparable results obtained in recent studies.

A deliberate decoloration approach is proposed, rooted in l*a*b* color space, 
utilizing the a* and b* components as color indicators, with an a*b* magnitude 
function mirroring the Euclidean distance. By incorporating decimal speed, this 
method emulates the effectiveness of traditional chemical decoloration processes, 
yet allows for precise control over color removal. The aforementioned concept 
is referred to as hue temperature-based decoloration (HTD), characterized by its 
performance, efficiency, and versatility across various tone mapping scenarios. 
In comparison to existing methods, TDm, a widely-used technique, is demonstrated 
to operate as a special instance of HTD. Through a combination of theoretical 
justification, in-depth analysis, and both subjective and objective evaluations, 
TDm's limitations and HTD's advantages are elucidated, with HTD's efficacy 
further optimized via an analysis of its internal workings.

We analyze the asymptotic behavior of a modified exponential function, $\exp\left(-\frac{z}{1-w}\right)$ on the complex plane. This behavior is modeled by a sequence of entire functions, $\phi_n(z)$, which correspond to the first $n+1$ terms of its exponential Taylor expansion. For a fixed $w$ with $|w|<1$, we demonstrate that $\phi_n(z)$ exhibits different growth characteristics depending on the magnitude of the argument of $z$. Specifically, $\phi_n(z)$ is entirely finite and displays exponentially bounded growth in a specific region. Moreover, we show that as $n$ increases, $\phi_n(z)$ converges to its limiting value with exponential speed within its region of uniform convergence. We prove a key property of $\phi_n(z)$, which states that for a given $z$, the distance between $\phi_n(z)$ and its limiting value decays exponentially with the mixing length, $n|w|$. Utilizing saddle point methods, we obtain a more in-depth understanding of the residual growth at the boundary of the mixing region. We further extend our findings to show that a modified residual growth at an optimal point beyond the mixing radius leads to an optimal residual analysis. Lastly, we illustrate the practical applications of these results in understanding the finite Padé table of the function $\frac{1}{1-w}.

We demonstrate the existence of a harmonic map with branch points from a Riemann surface of infinite genus with countable surfaces of non-positive curvature attached to its boundary, to a CAT($k$) space. This map is branched, and its support has a non-empty interior in the Riemann surface. Moreover, if it is not constant, it provides a homeomorphic embedding of the surface into the surface of non-positive curvature. This result generalizes previous findings on unbranched maps and their uniformization properties.

The development of laser technology with high peak power is being applied to various scientific fields such as nuclear, particle and quantum physics. This paper presents a new approach based on this concept and develops a comprehensive simulation framework to study laser interactions with plasma to generate quantum electrodynamics phenomena. We begin with a theoretical analysis of laser interactions to find a conditions under which it maximizes the plasma light emission. We present computational results showcasing various quantum electrodynamics phenomena produced by laser interactions with plasma under strong magnetic fields. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this technique can recreate conditions similar in magnitude to the Standard Model, allowing scientists to observe theoretical predictions such as birefringence caused by vacuum fluctuations in the presence of extremely strong magnetic fields.

This research examines the theoretical predictions and experimental constraints on the 2HDM model that includes Yukawa couplings, adhering to a discrete $Z_2$ symmetry, which can either be conserved or broken. The study focuses on the impact of the 2HDM's order parameter, denoted as $m_{12}$, on its spectrum of Higgs bosons and the resulting limits on this parameter, considering tree-level predictions and one-loop corrections. The model under consideration encompasses the Type-I and Type-II fermion coupling structures. The analysis involves an in-depth examination of the 2HDM spectrum within a comprehensive parameter space. Key observations include: Firstly, the 2HDM at high masses exhibits a pseudo-real spectrum, where the Higgs boson spectrum closely mirrors that of the SM, with the heavy Higgs bosons exhibiting neutral orientations. Secondly, confirmed Higgs decay measurements at the LHC impose stringent bounds on the 2HDM, particularly when the Higgs boson mass approaches the top quark mass and the 2HDM develops an imaginary order parameter. Thirdly, an imaginary order parameter is found to be disallowed in the Type-I fermion coupling structure, where the top quark becomes complex, in accordance with the model's symmetry requirements. The shift from anonymous XSD types to gRSDS expressions enables better representation of complex relationships in RDF graphs. This improvement arises due to the inherent capability of gRSDS expressions to capture the semantics of XSD cardinality constraints and union choices through 3 and n-ary relationships, respectively. A new approach is proposed for creating gRSDS-constrained RDF data, replacing anonymous XSD instances with gRSDS shape expression references. A 3-SAT compliant RDF verification query is designed to detect violations against these expressions. An actual case study, involving the digital preservation of XLS spreadsheets, demonstrates that utilizing gRSDS shape expressions is effective in accurately modeling XSD constraints. Shape analysis can be used to enforce these constraints without relying on XSLT or XT-XSD, while also enabling constraint validation over existingXSLS XLS-to-RDF conversions.

To accurately estimate a function's nonparametric regression in the presence of noise, we've developed a versatile boundary estimation toolkit with a balanced approach to speed and accuracy. Our proposed solution is a library called pyStoNED, which uses a distribution-based estimation technique to solve for a function's convex or concave form through a convex optimization process. The library offers a range of versatile functions to estimate the underlying function's boundary in various situations, including those with irregular data, irregular noise, irregular boundaries, and irregular data points. The library's methods have been thoroughly validated through extensive numerical experiments, demonstrating a significant improvement in speed and accuracy compared to a traditional kernel-based approach. The library's versatility and ease of use make it a valuable tool for data analysis in various fields of study.

Our investigation into the process where a Higgs boson is produced alongside a top-antitop pair at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) reveals that cross sections for this process exceed those of direct Higgs production at factor of a few for Higgs masses up to 135 GeV. This finding holds significant potential for detecting the Higgs in the 0- to 135-MeV mass range beyond its direct line of sight. A key feature of this process involves an enhanced taggability of top antitop events due to photons produced in association with leptons, allowing for a more precise reconstruction of Higgs momentum. Leptonic decays significantly contribute taggability over nearly the entire mass spectrum examined, and interestingly, our results indicate no substantial change in taggability over the Higgs mass spectrum due to potential interference with $W$ boson triangle loop processes. By employing taggability corrections to improve resolution and reducing background interference through photon energy spectrum analysis and higher mass requirements on detected objects, we find that effective cross sections can be reduced by factors of a few. This approach leads to a detectable signal separation from background at 5 sigma confidence level with 300 inverse femtobarn LHC luminosity, and a Higgs detection is feasible at just 100 inverse femtobarn luminosity.

We evaluate the performance of unsupervised and few-shot analysis using pre-trained language models across six benchmark datasets, covering a range of tasks including clustering, anomaly detection, sentence classification, word sense disambiguation, sentence pair classification, and sentence compression. Our largest dataset comprises over 3 million sentences from the LangLang benchmark, which we believe should be made publicly available. Additionally, we find that simple fine-tuning techniques yield substantial performance improvements over unsupervised analysis and few-shot prompts for pre-trained models.

The primary goal of this project is to create a resource of speech recognition models for the German language, leveraging the Open Source version of Kaldi as the technical foundation. Additionally, it encompasses the development of a community-driven platform to facilitate collaboration among users seeking to enhance the speech recognition capabilities for German. Kaldi will be used as the technical backbone for the project. Key components will include pre-trained acoustic models and word embeddings that can be easily adapted to various datasets and require minimal configuration. To support community involvement, Open Source speech recognition projects for German are encouraged. To assist users in customizing the system for specific domains, Kaldi will be used as the technical backbone for the project. Kaldi's flexibility allows for easy customization of the speech recognition models to various datasets and requirements with minimal configuration.

The 30 Doradus nebula, known for its massive Be stars, allows us to study these fast-rotating B-type stars in detail using data from the VLT/MUSE. Our analysis of 80 Be stars, combined with a custom code, reveals that these stars have moderate rotation speeds, with equatorial velocities ranging from 200 to 300 km/s. However, a few exceptional stars, including VFTS 182, exhibit even higher rotation speeds. Our findings also indicate that the mass-loss rates of these Be stars are significantly higher than those of their B main sequence counterparts, with mean values exceeding $10^{-8} M_\odot/yr$. Interestingly, the distribution of mass loss rates is skewed, with some stars exhibiting higher rates. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the Be stars' wind properties, measured by parameter P, are consistent with a standard wind model proposed by de Becker & Majaess. A notable trend is observed where stars with higher mass loss rates tend to be hotter and bluer. A lack of correlation is found between mass loss rates and spectral classification or luminosity classes. Finally, our analysis also indicates that the Be stars' wind parameters, especially P, are correlated with their rotational velocities.

Contrary to traditional text standardization, which involves manually creating rules, data-driven inverse text standardization (ITST) aims to revert standardized texts to their original forms, utilizing data and its statistical properties to improve comprehension and efficacy in various natural language processing tasks, such language models and named entity recognition. However, benchmark data for ITST is limited, and relies on manually created rules, thereby capping its effectiveness. Our study explores enhancing data-driven ITST by employing data augmentation techniques that involve composing, reordering, and substituting text, thereby improving model performance in both word and subword settings through word and subword embeddings. Our research also reveals that ITST rules should be developed through composition rather than substitution to avoid introducing inconsistencies in the original data. Our results demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform the state-of-the-art data-driven ITST models.

This paper demonstrates a variant of the Faber-Krahn inequality for the Hermite operator applied to domains with Robin boundary conditions, showing that as the parameter tends to infinity, these sets converge to specific geometric shapes called "cylinders" defined by the expression $x_1^2+\dots +x_d+\{1\}, x_d\in\mathbb{R}$, and we also investigate the behavior of the first eigenvalue for these sets and its corresponding eigenfunctions.

In many fields, including computer vision and deep learning, kernels play a pivotal role in kernel-based techniques. The emergence of neural tangent kernels has allowed researchers to connect deep learning and kernel methods more effectively. However, the vast array of kernel designs has made it challenging to determine which kernels are suitable for specific tasks. In this research, we propose a novel class of kernels called non-exchangeable tangent kernels (NFT-Ks), which can be mathematically described using the neural tangent kernel formula. Unlike kernels that are exchangeable, NFT-Ks are adaptable to the data, which makes them particularly beneficial for complex data with intricate geometric structures. Through comprehensive experiments, we evaluated an adaptive kernel method using NFT-Ks, which achieved superior performance on various datasets when applied to tasks like logistic regression and SVM with different kernels, showcasing the value of kernels that are exchangeable-invariant.

The abundance of non-Hermitian topological phases presents an intriguing opportunity for developing new theoretical frameworks and practical applications. Researchers have been particularly focused on the unique non-Hermitian topological metal, characterized by its non-Hermitonic point gaps and remarkable particle-hole symmetry, within various unitary and disordered chains. Our study delves into the impact of non-Hermitian particle-hole and Haldane models exhibiting non-Hermitian point-gap topology when subjected to reduced Haldane model conditions. Our findings indicate that the one-dimensional non-Hermitian Haldane model's rich topological characteristics are diminished by the removal of certain terms. Notably, the non-Hermitian point-gap topology is eliminated within the reduced Haldane model, resulting in a transitional state that is analogous to the traditional Haldane phase found in Hermitian systems. Our research also identifies two distinct topological invariants - a non-Hermitian topological index derived in the unitary case and a Chern number obtained from a surface charge pump mechanism within the reduced Haldane model. These findings are substantiated by numerical simulations based on the driving time dynamics in the reduced Haldane model.

A recent 2021 study identified significant connections between characteristics in spoken language and a speaker's background. The research also demonstrated that these characteristics can be treated as elements within a unified framework using a specialized model called an embedding. Our research builds upon these findings by exploring the potential to incorporate a speaker's characteristics into cutting-edge speech synthesis methods. The investigation utilizes two approaches: an embedding-based method to map a speaker's characteristics to the most suitable parameters in advanced neural synthesis systems, and a method to generate this parameter set using the speaker's voice. The resulting model allows for the synthetic generation of speech that not only mimics a speaker's identity but also incorporates their characteristics in a natural, nuanced manner. The evaluation process involved both experiments that adjusted characteristics directly and tests that incorporated both direct modification and automatically generated parameters. The evaluations, which included assessments using listener panels and both controlled and natural scenarios, revealed that incorporating a speaker's characteristics not only had a positive impact but also prevented any decrease in the ability to recognize the speaker. Additionally, the evaluations demonstrated that synthetic speech could effectively convey the selected characteristics. The code supporting this research is available online at: https://github.com/speechly/embedded-social-attributes-synthesis.

A unique variant of a global $A_4$ symmetry has been proposed, unifying neutrino mass patterns with the generation of baryon asymmetry through CP violation. Meanwhile, another symmetry $U(1)_{B-L}$ is introduced, and its breaking is linked to the origin of neutrino masses via the seesaw mechanism and CP violation, in addition to initiating a first-order phase transition that produces luminous dark radiation. A luminous dark photon emerges as a consequence of $U(1)_{B-L}$, and the sphaleron process is activated by a scalar field to produce baryon asymmetry through CP-violating CP-even scalars. A model is introduced combining these concepts. A phase transition resulting from a $U(1)_{B-L}$ breaking can generate luminous dark radiation, and a complex Higgs doublet is required to achieve a desirable electroweak vacuum. A specific parameter space is selected to match a desirable light neutrino mass and generate a suitable vacuum, and this model is examined by electroweak precision tests and constraints from direct detection of dark matter. Electroweak precision tests confirm that dark matter candidates, including a heavy neutral lepton and a dark fermion, can coexist with a desirable light neutrino mass. As a consequence, the model predicts that a desirable light neutrino mass correlates with reduced constraints on a dark sector mass scale by factors of 10-1000.

Building on a previous approach where the minimum length principle was used to describe three-dimensional nuclei with non-zero spin ground states in  \cite{PRD},  the current study expands this method to the five specific cases under consideration. By applying the technique, we obtain a minimum value for Planck's constant's lower bound, $\sqrt{10}\times10^{-16}$ for all nuclei under examination.  The resulting bound provides good theoretical justification for incorporating an anharmonic term into the harmonic oscillator potential for nuclei where $\kappa=16$ or lower.  By incorporating minimum length principle, we modify the three-dimensional Schrödinger equation for three-body nuclear systems, leading to a finite lower bound for the binding energy and implying that triangular combinations of three nucleons cannot be bound, regardless of the input parameters used.

This paper explores the properties of Golay complementary sets in a generic creational framework, where specific identities serve as the underlying basis. A particular instance of this general structure is Golay complementary sequences. Notably, certain combinations of three or more sets can generate Golay complementary collections, whereas pairs are less prevalent. To address this restriction, we demonstrate that any three creational pairs result in Golay complementary sets of three with an increased size, specifically of n(n-1)/2. A particular subset of these sets, of n(n-1)/2-2 in size, exists for all even values of n. A novel application of our findings reveals the generation of triplets of locally optimal CP polyphase sets.

In the field of aerospace intelligence, security, and environmental analysis, researchers are increasingly relying on advanced hyperspectral imaging technology. A critical application of this technology involves altering image features, which demands precise detection capabilities. In this study, investigators employed a cutting-edge approach, which integrates multiple deep convolutional autoencoders and is capable of operating without extensive labeled data. The proposed technique involves training multiple autoencurers on separate hyperspectral image collections, which are then utilized to produce features and combine them in order to evaluate alterations. The outcome shows promising results compared to previous approaches.

A broad range of molecular interactions were employed for spherical particles 
to study the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity in liquid states. 
This relationship appears applicable to various molecular models, yet it fails for 
a specific type of interaction characterized by highly asymmetric potentials. 
In the successful cases, it is demonstrated that viscous contributions are dominated 
by repulsive forces, a notion previously proposed, with residual entropy being a reliable 
measure of this influence. A comparative analysis between simple atomic fluids and complex 
molecular models was also conducted, revealing similarities but also key distinctions 
between their transport properties. Notably, these differences are primarily attributed to 
anisotropic interactions between molecular parts, a phenomenon not significant in pure 
atomic fluids.

The standard $\Lambda CDM$ cosmological model has been modified by replacing the eternal expansion with a new cyclical model featuring repeated periods of contraction and expansion. A mathematical model has been created that measures the complexity of each cycle using the number of e-folds, an important cosmological indicator of expansion. To evaluate past e-folds, the baryon acoustic oscillation and Hubble data have been used to determine the present value of the Hubble constant and other cosmological parameters. Results show that the model can achieve a good fit with current data without using a flatness parameter, yielding similar results to those of the standard model in terms of maximum likelihood and confidence intervals. This model also matches a linear relationship between the present size of the universe and the number of e-folds across multiple cycles. Additionally, the model has an advantage in avoiding the fine-tuning problem associated with the standard model's contraction phase, eliminating the need for a large, empty universe in its early stages.

The Invariant-set hypothesis, proposed by superdeterminists, claims that the universe operates within a set of immutable rules that govern all events. We scrutinize this idea using classical bits as visible variables and super-terabits as hidden variables to conclude that for a vast network of hidden variables even slightly smaller than a single byte, visible phenomena must align on a geometric structure comprising the most basic building blocks, making them visible to us.

In recent years, neural networks have achieved keyphrase detection success, but their size and intricacy make them impractical on modern IoT devices. This paper outlines techniques to execute these networks on constrained hardware. First, we assess the feasibility of running state-of-the-art neural networks on modern IoT devices. Second, we demonstrate a method to transform a GPU-based convolutional neural network into a portable binary format, utilizing the TensorRT accelerator. Third, we optimize the memory usage of such networks through memory pruning, a process that identifies and discards unnecessary weights. Fourth, we illustrate how to efficiently execute pruned networks on the ARM Cortex-A53 CPU. Fifth, we show the effectiveness of a convolutional-subspace-transformer architecture in achieving keyphrase detection. Sixth, we evaluate the balance between the accuracy and efficiency of this architecture and its CPU and GPU counterparts. Lastly, we demonstrate how the ARM Cortex-A53 CPU can compete with the TensorRT-optimized GPU, resulting in a 30% decrease in power consumption, a 50% reduction in model size, and a 30% reduction in execution time.

In a non-relativistic two-dimensional system of neutral dimers subjected to a periodic potential, we have developed an accurate theoretical model that predicts the system's behavior when charged for any degree of charge. Notably, we discovered that a gauge field interacts naturally with this system, resulting in the emergence of a Dirac fermion with a finite density when in a critical state. The gauge's influence on the system is noteworthy, as it broadens the dimers' energy spectrum in a way that is proportional to the square root of the gauge field's magnitude. The properties of these charged dimers are remarkably governed by relativistic physics, with this model exhibiting behavior similar to a two-dimensional equivalent of a Weyl system. In an experimentally realizable environment, we examined the system when placed in a homogeneous magnetic field, finding that for a non-zero charge density and zero gauge field, a non-zero complex susceptibility is exhibited by the system.

In numerous real-world applications, zero-inflation and sparse data are frequently encountered challenges. Existing techniques for dealing with these issues often assume a continuous and Gaussian distribution for the data. However, in many scenarios, the data may follow different distributions and have no a priori sparsity. To address these limitations, a novel approach has been developed that allows for flexible distributional assumptions and incorporates a group Lasso framework for variable selection and handling zero-inflation. By adapting the Group Lasso framework to handle nominal data, this approach leverages the inherent group structure of the data. It was successfully tested on simulated datasets spanning various model families and real-world datasets, including some with a high dimensionality. The proposed approach outperformed established techniques and a simulation study further validated its efficacy and achieved impressive results under both nominal and misspecified settings, while offering a computation-efficient solution.

As the potential for embedded real-time systems based on general-purpose processors grows due to advancements in technology, ensuring seamless execution of critical tasks becomes essential. To effectively secure these systems, high-performance isolated virtualization technologies like Intel VT-x must be utilized. Nevertheless, conventional isolated virtualization lacks in providing robust security, necessitating for dedicated hypervisors such as T-Visor, which assigns a unique security level to each execution domain. To accommodate evolving demands, T-Visor needs to facilitate various security domains, each possessing distinct levels of security priority. Consequently, a modified version of T-Visor, incorporating the concept of differing task importances, is presented to enhance the versatility of embedded real-time systems.

Panoramic stitching remains an open challenge when dealing with extensive environments characterized by large camera rotations and corresponding distortions in line features. In such instances, many coordinate systems are potential solutions, resulting in a ambiguous match selection process. Many features, including horizontal vanishing points, are influenced by vertical features and exhibit parabolic curves due to lens perspective and the gravitational influence. Our proposed approach leverages the understanding of these environmental constraints to establish a consistent match selection for line segments. By utilizing a prior knowledge of gravity, vertical features, and lens properties, we transform line fitting into an optimal matching problem governed by simple physical principles, thereby ensuring match robustness against perturbations and providing interpretative insights. Our method's parameter requirements are minimal and can be inferred from images or set based on user-defined camera models and image calibration. Furthermore, it's an extensible framework, easily adaptable to incorporate additional prior knowledge, and forms the basis of a panoramic stitching method, which can be used even when the environment is not predominantly vertical.

Chimeric states, in which identical subgroups exhibit the same behavior while remaining distinct, are observed within larger populations of heterogeneous oscillators.  A reduction in the system to two groups allows for a detailed analysis of the state's emergence, in which, due to the interconnected nature of the groups, one group remains synchronized according to an external reference, whereas the other group oscillates autonomously.  We investigate the behavior of systems consisting of two large groups of oscillators, in which parameter variations within each group follow a uniform probability distribution.  We show that as the number of oscillators tends towards infinity, the probability distribution of phases, in chimeric states, converges to a uniform distribution over a circular domain, validating previous research using numerical simulations and analytical methods based on finite-size corrections.

When controlling a dynamic system, the presence of unknown disturbances can lead to loss of control. To counter this, researchers have developed controllers that can withstand disturbances. This work focuses on the model-free method of designing such resilient controllers for linear systems subject to stochastic disturbances. By ensuring a lower bound on the probability that the state remains within a constrained region, the proposed approach ensures a guaranteed level of constraint satisfaction. This technique ensures optimal performance in the absence of disturbances and resilience when disturbances are present, by seeking a policy that maximizes the minimum probability of remaining within the safe set, while staying as close to the original optimal policy as possible. Since this problem is difficult to solve directly, a novel algorithmic approach, named Probabilistic Model-Driven Policy Search, is proposed. This method transforms the challenging problem into a sequence of more tractable linear programming problems, enabling efficient implementation. Through both theoretical analysis and simulation, the approach's effectiveness is demonstrated, and it is shown to outperform existing methods, especially when the disturbance distribution is unknown.

Recently, a higher slice ring was introduced as an adaptation of the usual slice ring concept in link theory. A further expansion of the theory was made, involving multi-layer diagrams and a corresponding family of multi-layer slice groups. Building upon recent advancements in multi-layer link theory, multi-layer slice and hyper slice knots were defined as the knots associated with the multi-layer slice group. A new multi-layer diagram invariant was then defined and proven to be stronger than existing multi-layer link invariants. Finally, it was demonstrated that the multi-layer diagrams give rise to multi-layer slice and hyper slice knot invariants.

We introduce an updated concept of entropy in the MERA tensor network, called refracted entropy, to describe entanglement entropy in systems undergoing chaotic time evolution. Within this framework, we calculate the time-dependent behavior of the refracted entropy in free boson systems with mappable typical states, revealing characteristics of the Page curve. Furthermore, we establish a typical entanglement spectrum for merged regions of size $l$ that grows logarithmically according to 2D geometry. Additionally, we broaden the definition of refracted entropy to apply to general quantum systems, and observe its alignment with coarse-grained holographic entropy in systems exhibiting chaotic time evolution.

Understanding systems composed of numerous interacting components is a significant objective of modern science.  The dynamics of these systems are influenced not only by their initial states but also by random fluctuations and the specific arrangements of their constituents. As a result, it is expected that different realizations of the same system will exhibit significantly different behaviors.  However, scientific studies have found that certain system characteristics can be transmitted from one generation to the next and are immune to the disruptive effects of random fluctuations and varying initial conditions.  This phenomenon is known as order-order transitions.  Our analysis reveals that for a class of interacting system models called cellular automata, a substantial portion of its order-order transition structures can be explained through entropy-based reasoning.  The characteristics of these transmissions are reminiscent of those found in thermally-driven processes.  In addition to order-order transmission, our findings also indicate the potential for initial conditions to have a lasting impact on the system's behavior. Furthermore, our study will be further expanded by applying its concepts to investigate transmission patterns in a broader range of interacting system models.

This paper introduces and investigates a novel variant of the H\'{e}non map from three dimensions, focusing on its underlying algebraic structure and inverse operation. Key features of the modified map are derived, specifically in relation to its use of an inverse matrix whose determinant equals one, ensuring the preservation of a particular surface, $\xi + \eta + \zeta = 2/3$. The study also examines the influence of matrix entries and initial conditions on orbit behavior in the variant map.

We demonstrate that requiring a Hamiltonian flow on the cotangent bundle of the Lorentz group, defined by a specific combination of generators and canonical momentum, to maintain the subgroup $SO(2,1)$ invariant is sufficient to uniquely determine the version of the holonomy employed in the Poincaré group context within the context of the AdS universe. This, in conjunction with existing arguments, results in the conclusion that this unique version corresponds to the holonomic approach.

We are examining the limits of the probability distributions whose statistics are restricted to specific values; specifically, we look at standard Young tableaux, where the number of hook lengths is a multiple of either two or three.

The Larmor clock tunneling duration was calculated based on the change in spin Larmor angle resulting from Pauli blocking. Our research demonstrates that the alternative tunneling duration, derived from spin Larmor angle, differs from the standard Larmor clock duration when the Larmor precession is dominated by spin Larmor. We compared the new duration with the existing Larmor clock duration and found they converge when the energy uncertainty is comparable to the barrier height.

In a nonrelativistic framework, the dominant twist-3 distribution profiles for P-wave mesons are derived from QCD meson distribution amplitudes, with their moments calculated and key features such as inflection points and zero-crossings identified. It is found that the $\phi$ p-wave oscillating profile amplitudes are significantly smaller than S-wave amplitudes, leading to the p-wave PSEUDOMOMENT becoming much larger than the P-MOMENT. Moreover, the $\phi$ p-wave profile exhibits a pronounced zero-crossing at around 30% PSM. By applying the $\phi$ p-wave oscillating profile to P-wave charmonia $\left|T_{J^P\;(2S+L,J)^{\chi}}(z)\right|$, it is determined that $\left|T_{^{1}P_J(2S+L,J^{\chi}=1)(z)\right|$ amplitudes have a zero-crossing at around 0.5 FM. Conversely, $\left|T_{^{3}P_J(2S+L,J^{\chi}=3)(z)\right|$ monotonically increasing profiles have a local extremum at around 0.65 FM. Importantly, the CTEQ-11 p-wave p-MOMENT to PSEUDOMOMENT ratio closely matches our $\phi$ p-wave P-MOMENT to PSEUDOMOMENT ratio

The behavior of Bose-Einstein condensates is analyzed for systems comprising two or more species of atoms, revealing a nonlinear Raman quantum switch analogous to a classical device. Furthermore, it's demonstrated that this system can function as a Raman filter.

We've re-examined the link between large diffeomorphisms atscripthr andscripthr infinity and the S-matrix by revisiting the crucial observation that the 1-loop "double soft" amplitude is equivalent to the Lie algebra of large diffeomorphisms known as the BMS algebra. In doing so, we clarify the underlying assumptions and clarify the connection between these theories, ultimately highlighting the circular reasoning present in earlier research regarding this relationship.

To achieve continuous learning in real-time while training a single model, the concept of an ensemble of models is utilized, where multiple sub-models are instantiated and merged to produce output, allowing the model to adapt and prevent catastrophic forgetting, maintain feature extraction, and improve prediction accuracy. This paper introduces a novel neural architecture, the Structure for Online Ensemble Learning (SOEL), and demonstrates its effectiveness, efficiency, and adaptability for various tasks. Specifically, it showcases how this architecture enables the model to accommodate multiple classes, maintain data integrity, and generalize effectively, while also facilitating improved feature representation and knowledge transfer between datasets.

To deepen the link between Topological Tversky similarity and Gromov-Hausdorff distance, we establish a generalized shape operator that takes any number of points on a metric space into consideration. Our findings demonstrate an equivalence between the Huisken-Ilmanen Shape operator and this new operator and its measure for probabilistic distributions. Moreover, the non-increasing property of its eigenvalues during the Ricci flow is preserved for four-dimensional metric space with fixed points, and we utilize this property to define an algorithm for finding Ricci flat metrics on products of two circles with varying parameters.

In this paper, we investigate permutation functions with complete mappings over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ for odd values of $q$, leveraging properties from number theory to identify certain cyclotomic permutations over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. Our approach yields several novel examples of permutation functions and permutation triple(s) over $\mathbb{Q}^{3}$. Notably, employing the difference set technique, we establish that there exist at least $\frac{4}{3} \cdot 10^{6}$ distinct permutation triple(s) over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ when $q$ is an even number. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that there exist permutation functions over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ possessing difference set properties for odd prime powers $q$. Importantly, these findings address an open query proposed by Dong et al. in their 2018 publication.

The ongoing threat of intestinal worm infections worldwide, particularly in developing nations,
drives research into effective diagnostic methods. Traditional diagnostics often rely on
identifying the worms in stool samples, a task that demands expertise and experience.
However, advanced technology has made it possible to use Deep Belief Features (DBF), a form
of feature extraction, to analyze the texture and structural characteristics of worms in
stool samples. Our research involves creating input images from the Hessian transformation
of the raw samples, and then using a Deep Belief Network (DBN) to identify worms. Our
results indicate a 91% accuracy in the classification of worms, highlighting the potential
of DBN as a feature extractor.

This research introduces a type of non-cooperative game within a regime-switching jump diffusion framework for concurrent investment and reinsurance decisions by a single insurer. Each player aims to maximize the insurer's value while the other seeks to maximize their individual profit. A dynamic programming approach is used to formulate the simultaneous optimization problem's solution, whose existence and uniqueness are proven through a L\'evy's Little Lemma. Moreover, the estimator proposed in this study can efficiently estimate the insurer's value while reinsurance premiums are strategic for both players.

Our research introduces a novel flight path planning method based on dual simplex algorithms to identify energy-efficient and stable flight paths for UAVs, with capabilities to evade obstacles in real-time flight environments. In our approach, we first reformulate the non-linear problem as a linear optimization task using polynomial interpolation, followed by relaxation using a genetic algorithm. To enhance the robustness of the planning method, we incorporate additional noise from a genetic algorithm and apply digital filter smoothing to filter out unwanted signals, resulting in a stable flight path. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted a real-world experiment involving a quadcopter that found an optimal flight path through a multi-dimensional space, demonstrating that our method significantly reduces power consumption compared to traditional digital filter smoothing techniques. Furthermore, we showcase our system's ability to process and adapt to real-world flight environments.

We present a comprehensive overview of pion-nucleon interactions below 500 MeV, beginning with a review of the fundamental concepts, followed by an explanation of the principles underlying the theory. Beyond that, established methods for analyzing data are discussed, along with a demonstration of how to perform a model-independent characterization utilizing chiral effective field theory constraints. Finally, various phenomenological nucleon and pion responses are compared against actual measurements, serving as a benchmark for evaluating low-energy nucleon-nucleon effective field theories.

In the search for new, rare, or elusive phenomena, improving the resolution of particle tracking plays a crucial part in boosting the overall event analysis sensitivity. The CMS detector's highly granulated pixel subdetector is particularly adept at producing high-resolution tracks, but this capability is hindered by a longstanding challenge: noise misidentifications in outer pixel modules. Past experiments have proposed various solutions to overcome this problem, which this research aims to further investigate. The CMS detector's upgrade, finalized in 2019, is designed to withstand higher radiation levels, higher collision energies, and a significantly higher luminosity. The CMS detector will also be read out in much faster timeframes, a feature that poses additional reconstruction challenges, particularly when dealing with hits near the edge of modules. The CMS detector's upgraded timing capabilities, coupled with its enhanced granularity, could potentially increase the resolution of track momentum. However, issues related to noise and false hits near the edge of modules will likely be more pronounced in the new CMS capabilities, and evaluating the impact of these factors is an essential step in the reconstruction process. The research presented here investigates and validates the performance of a new technique, utilizing a multivariate clustering method, to improve the efficiency of reconstructing tracks, and its potential to increase the momentum resolution. The research utilized CMS simulation and data from the CMS Phase-1 Pilot Edge dataset. The results indicate that implementing the multivariate clustering method results in a notable improvement in the resolution of track momentum.

Active galactic nuclei powered by supermassive black holes in the past exhibit significant influence on the universe's cosmic background and galaxy evolution. Investigating active galactic nuclei at redshift less than one reveals information about these power sources and allows for the exploration of their connections with galaxy evolution. Morphological studies of active galactic nuclei reveal that their morphology often resembles early-stage galaxy morphologies and is more distinct from non-active galaxies at low redshifts. We employ two machine intelligence methods to analyze the morphology of 100,000 active galactic nuclei in the Hyper Supirime-Cam Wide Survey, finding that our results align with previous research. Moreover, our research reveals differences in the morphology-harmonic relation between active and non-active galaxies, suggesting that galaxy active galactic nuclei interactions result in more complex morphologies.

At low-momentum transfers, atomic collisions often yield notable short-range correlations between two particles. This research involves generating momentum distributions for pairs of particles, as well as their corresponding Wigner distributions, to describe correlations between helium-deuterium and helium-tritium combinations. These calculations are based on the Avrigescu et al. four-body wave function. A strong relationship exists between the momentum and Wigner distributions. This research further demonstrates that the form of the distribution depends heavily on the choice made. Despite variations, all explored forms share a common spatial feature: a pronounced, large-scale correlation surrounded by smaller-scale ripple effects. These effects highlight the critical role of the hard-core component of the nucleon-nucleon interaction, as revealed by ripple correlations.

Deep learning, utilizing complex numbers, has the potential to be highly effective in problems such as time-series forecasting and multichannel signal processing, where its advantages are significant due to the inherent benefits of the complex domain, for instance by eliminating real and imaginary components as separate entities. Current research, however, is hindered by the limitations of vanishing gradients and the lack of support for complex comparisons in deep learning frameworks, which hinders the exploitation of complex-valued representations for identifying complex-valued targets. We propose the complex domain equality loss to address these challenges, a straightforward to implement technique that transforms complex comparison into real and imaginary parts while preserving the inherent complex structure, and demonstrate its effectiveness through an implementation of deep complex-valued long short-term memory networks for multichannel signal prediction, where it significantly outperforms its real-valued counterparts achieved an impressive improvement of approximately 10%.

The low-metallicity stars in the Galactic halo and the dwarf spheroidal galaxy, Segue 1, display an unexplained wide abundance spread of various elements. To shed light on this spread and gain insight into the chemical development of early low-metallicity systems, we created two modified Boda simulations. We altered the standard model by adjusting key parameters, such as the mass of gas inflows and the time frame of star formation. By including a longer gas inflow of moderate mass in our modified standard model, we were able to account for abundance spread in certain intermediate-mass stars. However, this model was unable to account for elements such as oxygen and magnesium differences seen in stars with a mass of approximately one solar unit. In contrast, our modified non-standard model, which simulated a short burst of star formation over 30 million years, successfully explained abundance spread in both high-mass and low-mass stars. This model suggests that early systems experienced a brief burst of star formation triggered by a gas inflow, followed by quiescence before another gas inflow triggered the formation of the current stars. Our high-resolution simulation, which models chemical development over 1.4 billion years, also shows wide abundance spread, particularly for elements such as oxygen and magnesium differences seen in stars with a mass of approximately one solar unit. This research introduces a comprehensive toolbox, dubbed EVALIT, for measuring numerical forecast quality, focusing on probability estimates like classification and ranking predictions. Our method assesses the sensitivity of calibrated forecasts to sample size changes, correlating it to Brier and Rank Brier scores. It is an alternative approach to Brier diffusion, adaptable to imbalanced samples and more efficient for large datasets. We apply this tool to assess key machine learning algorithms, utilizing variables from the PSID to predict financial literacy, identifying SVM and KNN algorithms as the highest-scoring models, despite Poisson regression being the top-performing model in overall performance, highlighting the value of secondary datasets for forecasting model development.

This study proposes a Quantum Computing Learning (QCL) framework, specifically employing SQUID-based QCs, to tackle complex learning challenges. We leverage the inherent quantum properties of SQUIDs, including superconductivity and flux quantization, to develop a QCL framework. In (2+1)D or (3+)D SQUID networks, we exploit the inherent quantum characteristics for efficient computation by applying specific magnetic flux to manipulate qubit states. We also introduce an QCO (Quantum Coin Operator) that enables exploitation of quantum non-locality. Our QCL framework integrates a QCO to connect a quantum processor with a learning machine, allowing for efficient solving of learning problems. We have integrated a QCO into a quantum circuit and paired it with a two-layer, ReLU-activated, machine with binary output to create a hybrid QC-ML solver. We evaluate the proposed QCL framework on a 2+1D SQUID network with an QCO, comparing its hybrid QC-ML solutions to those of standard machine learning models on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets. Notably, our hybrid QC-ML solution rivals the performance of the advanced ResNet52 model on the challenging CIFAR10 dataset, showcasing promising accuracy and a proposed quantum non-local effect that significantly enhances the model's performance.

Two novel distorted product structures have been proposed and definitions for distorted product near-Kahler and nearly contact manifolds proposed. We examine the distorted product submanifolds of nearly contact manifolds, investigating their geometric characteristics in four nearly contact metric fibered product types: purely slant, pure slant, product slant with a rank of 1, and products involving a 1-dimensional slant submanifold. We also study purely slant distorted product submanifolds for certain nearly contact metric fibered products. Additionally, we define and study distorted product pointwise slant normal integral submanifolds of nearly contact Riemannian manifolds, investigating their geometric properties in three submanifolds: pointwise slant warped products, pointwise slant product with a rank of 1, and pointwise product warped involving a 1-dimensional slant submanifold. We establish relationships between distorted product pointwise slant warped product submanifolds and warped product theories. We study purely slant distorted product submanifolds in the standard contact sphere, spherical space form, and Euclidean space, identifying constraints for specific submanifold types in these spaces.

Diamond's defect structures exhibit the ability to detect and record radiation exposure, making them suitable instruments for detecting and measuring low energy nuclear recoil events. While the research primarily focuses on high-energy particles and rare, inactive nuclear recoil radiation, this study aims to explore the applicability of using the Kramers-Kronig analysis on the photoluminescence emission spectra to study and measure N3 color centers in detecting low-energy nuclear recoil events. This was achieved by utilizing an electron beam to stimulate the N3 defects in a controlled laboratory setting composed of nitrogen impurities in a nitrogen-rich lattice structure, followed by heat treatment. Moreover, our research found the photoluminescence emission spectra to be sensitive to the lattice damage caused by helium-3 atoms, generated through the laboratory-induced nuclear reaction of deuterium and helium-3. This unusual sensitivity to the low-energy nuclear recoil events could potentially be utilized to assess radioactive contamination in the environment.

We examine the movement of a particle within an uneven environment using mathematical tools derived from Brownian motion. Our analysis shows that a steady current can emerge within a confined space due to this nonuniformity, even though the particle and environment themselves remain constant. Additionally, a method is devised to counteract the effect, eliminating current by adjusting a parameter. Our solution also allows us to calculate how an external obstacle influences the particle's mobility, providing insight into its "clogging" capabilities. As the obstacle becomes comparable in size to the particle, a specific threshold is reached where it effectively blocks its passage.

Researchers discovered an extensive array of highly stable fractional quantum Hall states governed by magnetorotonic coefficients up to c = 6, featuring clusters of a total of 24 states. Each of these states is characterized by a distinct magnetorotonic coefficient and a specific pattern of correlations among electrons within a 2D plane. Notably, states with higher magnetorotonic coefficients exhibit increased complexity and less reliance on short-range correlations. Notably, this study found two types of states - nonhierarchical states with considerable fluidic correlations and a total body order parameter, and hierarchical states arising from correlations of vortices and particles. Moreover, the study utilized a density matrix renormalization group technique in a 2D plane to analyze the energy spectra of multi-magnetorotonic states. This approach enabled the researchers to identify clear patterns in the distribution of spectral gaps and confirmed that multi-magnetorotonic states possess unique characteristics, such as higher degeneracy and distinct bodies.

We introduce an innovative approach for detecting and analyzing recurring patterns in networks, specifically in the context of rapidly spreading phenomena. In epidemiology, this approach can identify clusters connected by short network paths and bridge nodes that facilitate rapid disease transmission between them. Existing methods struggle with computing the distances required, but we overcomes this limitation by approximating the distances with network structures containing randomly distributed pathogens. Our approach utilizes these structures to identify outbreaks without pre-computing distances. We compare our method to a traditional clustering algorithm in simulation studies and demonstrate its superiority. Furthermore, we apply our approach to analyze the real-world dynamics of information transmission on networks.

When creating maximum likelihood maps for the Cosmic Microwave Background, low-signal areas surrounding high signal points can result in distorted, erroneous, and negatively valued pixels, a phenomenon known as the "X-es problem." To address this issue, an improved method involves including a low-multipole prior in the likelihood function, with the effectiveness of this approach being tied to whether the low-multipole term accurately reflects real foreground signals at low angular scales. This approach, however, fails to resolve X-es solely based on raw pixel values and works best when combined with cleaned, deconvoluted point sources, as it allows the method to draw on both the low and high signal point estimates to constrain pixel solutions, with the likelihood function then serving to regularize pixel errors, particularly in high-error areas. Furthermore, this approach's effectiveness relies on uncorrelated pixel estimation schemes over multi-resolution ones, as it enables the method to utilize maximum likelihood's area-averaging property to average pixel values within the area's radius, thus mitigating errors.

Developing goal-oriented models is a key challenge in robotics, and using language allows these models to be created quickly. Still, referring to specific objects within a task description can be ambiguous, resulting in inconsistent learning and actions, especially when multiple objects are present in a reference. We tackle this issue by introducing a general framework, enabling robots to perform everyday tasks such as placing an object on another, placing another item beside another, and cutting another item from another, thereby referring to multiple instances of reference. We accomplish this by assigning unique identifiers to multiple objects within images through color-coded segmentation, thus resolving the ambiguity of referring to specific objects within language instructions. We evaluate a newly developed goal-oriented model across various domains and instruction sets using three benchmarks and compare it to existing language-conditioned reinforcement learning baselines.

We introduce the concept of state and channel families being $k$-extendible and derive their classical and quantum information-theoretic properties as well as unique ways to describe and visualize them. A general method is developed to tomographically reconstruct quantum channels based on their extendibility. We apply this method to determine a class of single-qubit channels known as shadow processes, and show that channel extendibility relates to shadow process geometry. We examine these channels from multiple perspectives: a discrete framework where channels are segments on the Bloch sphere, continuous families of channels with spherical symmetry, mappings between these families based on the Bloch sphere's geometry, and the existence of reversible transformations preserving the distance within each family. We also establish a connection between a particular distance measure defined on single-qubit channel families and the distance measure defined on the shadows of these channels within the space of linear operators. Furthermore, we reveal that the channel that maximizes information transfer for any given initial quantum state within a shadow process family, is a completely depolarizing channel. We implement and demonstrate our methods through experiments on photonic quantum systems to support these findings.

For planar convex shapes, a specific geometric constant is defined and used to derive and prove refined versions of the isoperimetric inequality, which outperforms its original form in providing the least amount of area containing radius R. Also, it's found that the area of a disk can be compared to the area of a ball of radius R, in relation to the geometric constant, thus giving the bounds of the spectral values of the Dirichlet Laplacian for the shape. Furthermore, it's found that as the geometric constant approaches infinity, the spectral values have a particular asymptotic behavior and we propose a related conjecture involving the isochromatic function. Lastly, we describe an algorithmic method used to draw curves with minimum non-eigenvalue spectral values, and present a computer-generated figure illustrating these curves for an L-shaped shape.

This study explores the complex challenge of determining an optimal flight path for an UAV, taking into account its goal to collect data from targets within a limited timeframe, while considering its various resource limitations. An existing approach based on dynamic programming is reviewed and its performance tested against alternative strategies. Results indicate the viability of simpler alternatives, such as heuristic methods. This problem has various real-world applications, including agricultural treatments, biological sampling, and surveillance operations.

The critical coupling constant of interlayer tunneling in bilayer graphene, where the electron density varies via an external electric field, was determined through the renormalization group analysis. As the external field is applied, the electron's effective charge increases, leading to charge density waves at the Fermi surface that become divergent. This phenomenon, previously explored using the renormalization group analysis, exhibits the influence of varying external fields on the electron's properties, ultimately leading to the critical point where the interlayer tunneling coupling constant approaches the instability threshold. This critical coupling constant causes the system to transition into the metallic state, marking the boundary between the insulating and metallic phases.

We have conducted both experimental and theoretical investigations into the structural modifications of Sc2TbN@C80 on h-BN/Ni(111) substrates driven by elevated temperatures. Our research utilized high-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy to visualize the molecule on the substrate, which exhibited a specific symmetry characteristic unique to its external orientation. Notably, this symmetry was observed to change when the temperature was raised to 320 K, resulting in a higher symmetry equivalent to C2v. Subsequent temperature increments caused the molecule to adopt a new conformation, characterized by a trimeric arrangement featuring a central molecule surrounded by three others. This phenomenon showcased evidence of molecule-molecule bonding, evidenced by the protrusions observed at bond lengths consistent with that seen in gas-phase scanning tunneling microscopy data. Furthermore, our research highlighted significant differences in ad-molecule heights and tunneling spectra between trimeric and monomeric arrangements, showcasing a 0.18 Angstrom reduction in tunneling current decay rate and the disappearance of resonance features, respectively.

This study assesses the efficacy of AES-ECB, Twofish-ECB, RIPERp, and RIPERs in safeguarding low energy IoT devices, with a focus on their susceptibility to attacks, particularly JPAs and CPA, using Tesla COIN coins as a model. The Twofish protocol exhibits strong resistance to these attacks and is not recommended for use with these IoT devices. In contrast, RIPERp and RIPERs have proven resilient in the context of a 5-coins JPA attack and a 5-coin CPA attack. However, the RIPERp and RIPERs protocols may become vulnerable under more extensive scenarios involving larger coin sets.

We developed a trial-assessment method to adaptively determine the optimal parameters for Ramsey measurements. After a preliminary test with initial settings, the procedure uses historical data to statistically evaluate and adjust parameters in subsequent trials. The goal is to maximize the sensitivity for clock-drift measurement by utilizing the standard Bayesian approach to analyze the results from each trial except the initial one. Based on the evaluation, we update the measurement parameters to optimize performance. Furthermore, the procedure was applied to real-world Atomic Penning Trap experiments to demonstrate its effectiveness in adjusting the measurement phase.

Network analysis has identified crucial nodes or regions through various centrality measures, and many networks have been studied using Gaussian random fields and network diffusion models. Our research proposes Gromov centrality, a new metric that uses the properties of triangle inequality more effectively for characterizing network properties. Gromov centrality comparisons are based on the application of Gromov hyperbolicity, specifically the δ parameter of Gaussian random fields. Our Gromov centrality is defined as the probability distribution of the Gromov-surplus generated by injecting a Gaussian field at a particular node. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated by evaluating its performance in identifying network field energy distributions, and we demonstrate its application on networks with known Gaussian field distributions.

A new metric tensor has been developed, allowing for an isotropic and isotropizable universe with a static distribution of matter. The energy-momentum tensor for this matter distribution was found to be unique, allowing further simplification by assuming zero components for $T_{0i}$. The resulting non-zero components for $T_{ii}$ exhibit the characteristics of an isotropic distribution. By considering the origin of the coordinate system, the metric tensor is found to have singularities only in the $z$ direction, making the azimuthal symmetry evident. This implies the gravitating mass resides on the $x-y$ plane. An expression relating pressure to density has been found, and it is found that when pressure approaches zero, a specific initial density value is reached at a particular radius.

Building upon previous research on rigorous equivalence of matrix pencils, we investigate the possible collections of matrix pencils that remain unchanged under rigorous equivalence. This involves examining transformations between matrix pencils, specifically those mapping each pair to one another, and determining which collections of matrix pencils admit such transformations. We extend the results from previously established work on isospectral pencils, proving that, except for the case of spectral pencils, no non-trivial collections of matrix pencils exist under rigorous equivalence. Moreover, for collections involving at least three matrix pencils, we establish that no non-trivial collections exist, and for pairs, for collections involving non-similar pencils, we demonstrate that no isospectral collections exist, and describe the properties of the set of isospectral collections. These results have implications for inverse spectral problems, showing that, except for the case of isospectral sets consisting of spectrally rigid pencils, no inverse spectral problem for discrete operator pencils is ill-posed. Furthermore, for collections involving non-similar pencils, no inverse spectral problem for discrete operator pencils is ill-posed.

We establish a general approach for defining T-duality within the framework of twisted tori utilizing Lie algebra deformation parameters, leading to the identification of two distinct duality groups: $Q = \mathbb{Z} \oplus Z$ and $Q^{\vee} = L \oplus Z^{\vee}$, characterized by a non-degenerate pairing $\langle -, \rangle$. The proposed method for T-duality is demonstrated with reference to $H$-spaces and specific Lie algebra deformation examples.

We derive a non-asymptotic upper bound for the worst-case distortion when embedding certain planar metrics into metrics with a small number of vertices. Specifically, every finite metric space that is pseudo-planar can be embedded into a metric with a graph structure in the range [n^(1/3 * alpha)/5, n^(1/3 + alpha)] for any given positive value of alpha, where the distortion depends on the number of vertices n. Here, "pseudo-planar" means the space can be represented as a subset of L1^3, and this property is true for all non-subgraph 2D metrics. As a direct result, all metrics with small edge isoperimetry can be embedded into O(n^(1/3 + alpha)) metric graphs with a bounded distortion, and in fact, graphs with small edge isoperimetry are inherently pseudo-planar. A subgraph 2D metric is a metric space where any subset can be represented as a subset of a 2D grid. A useful application of our findings is in graph theory, specifically in the proof that every finite pseudo-planar metric can be embedded into a metric with a graph structure in the range [n^(1/3 * alpha)] with a bounded distortion, and as a result, our findings imply an upper bound for the Euclidean planar graph embedding problem in terms of n^(1/3).

In a discrete-time system, every trajectory converges to a single, globally stable equilibrium under the condition of strong monotonicity. Research into the dynamics of monotonic systems, especially near stable equilibrium points, has a long history. Recent studies have revealed that a quadratic stability structure can arise in discrete-time systems even when the underlying continuous system is neutrally stable. Building upon existing studies, our research demonstrates that a higher-order quadratic or cubic stability structure can also occur due to perturbations, with these methods being applicable to discrete-time systems derived from continuous system discretizations. Furthermore, our research shows that a higher-order cubic or quadratic stability structure exists and is stable in discrete-time systems obtained from the midpoint method or trapezoidal rule. We also examine the impact of additional noise-like perturbations on the quadratic and cubic models and find that these perturbations can alter the order of stability, reducing it to either a cubic or quadratic structure.

The variational eigensolver is a key tool in quantum computing, but it has limitations in dealing with difficult problems. Our research presents an innovative adaptive version of the vari eigensolver that enhances its ability to find accurate ground states. The enhanced algorithm utilizes a unique ground-state ansatz that is built upon the system's first excited states, which is achieved by combining the vqc's unitary operator with the number operator in the excitation basis. By adding a term to the cost function that targets the overlap between the ansatz and the excited states, the adaptive algorithm ensures better mixing towards the target ground state. Testing this approach on hydrogen and beryllium molecules revealed that it can produce more accurate ground states than the original vqc, especially in complex molecular configurations.

A widely accepted approach in a deep learning architecture decodes deep latent space estimates to obtain local data representations. However, researchers challenge this assumption, citing multiple issues with this standard approach. Under certain conditions, this decoder can hinder the effectiveness of the entire network, especially when used in representation learning, due to certain structural limitations that make the decoder unable to capture crucial, high-dimensional data characteristics. As a result, this decoder often introduces learning difficulties and suboptimal overall network performance. To address this problem, the author proposes a groundbreaking 'generative decoder', derived from a different perspective, and proves its ability to generate samples drawn from a specific data distribution $ \mathcal{D} $ with the highest likelihood under specific assumptions, thus making it the best possible approach. To verify this innovative decoder's effectiveness, the author proposes a novel, straightforward, author-independent evaluation metric specifically designed to assess how well the decoder captures essential, high-dimensional data characteristics, and demonstrates its ability to significantly outperform existing approaches under specific, well-defined scenarios where it especially shines.

The Hubble tension may be resolved if a gravitational wave background significantly affects the determination of key parameters. If a GW background with a rigid amplitude of approximately 10^-9 exists across all frequencies, it can have a non-negligible impact on our understanding of early universe physics and other parameters, leading to a significant reduction in uncertainty for these values. Notably, a GW amplitude of around 10^-9 can create a constant spectrum across the sky, yet our Hubble tension findings contradict this scenario, ruling out the possibility of a GW background with a rigid amplitude of roughly 10^-9, consistent with NANOGrain and LIGO-Virgo observations.

Our observations, carried out using the Atacama Compact Array (ALMA), have provided a detailed map of molecular emissions in several key species as the inner region of transient comet C/2015 ER61 approached the Sun. These emissions include carbon monoxide, carbon monosulfide, water, and ammonia, and were collected nearly one week prior to the comet's perihelion. Notably, the observed spatial distribution of molecules suggests a distinct source of carbon monosulfide, contrasting with the uniform distribution of other molecules. This finding, along with estimates of total molecular output, has significant implications for understanding the physical and chemical processes occurring within the comet's nucleus.

We propose an efficient, unsupervised approach to speech synthesis that operates without the need for labeled data, significantly reducing computational costs. A generative model is designed to derive a linear transformation that maps acoustic units to an implicit speaker embedding space determined solely by the acoustic data. By utilizing a basic noise model as a prior, the method learns the inverse transformation as well as the acoustic-to-lexicon alignment in the implicit speaker embedding space using an adversarial framework, all in a supervised manner. The model's performance is comparable to current state-of-the-art projects, as evidenced by its achieved mean opentextile quality and intelligibility ratings of 22.62 and 4.62, respectively, on the Librispeech dataset. Notably, the method's implementation is straightforward and its performance gains can be attributed to its pre-processing step, which can be applied to any dataset with minimal computational overhead.

This article explores the effectiveness of Tsallis entropy as a tool for estimating the maximum mass of a galaxy cluster, a task previously undertaken by Holographic Dark Energy (HDE) and Matter Coupled Dark Energy (MCDE) models. A crucial aspect in these researches is the survival factor, a concept proposed for correcting galaxy number deficits in the observational data of redshift surveys. By setting up a novel model that accounts for Tsallis entropy's effects on the maximum mass of a cluster, researchers aim to reduce uncertainties in these estimates. To achieve this, researchers have considered two distinct scenarios, referred to as Complex Form of Quintessence (CFQ) and Recast Complex Form of Quintessence (RCQ), in order to investigate their implications for cosmological parameters. Scenarios CFQ1 and CFQ2 are characterized by positive values of the survival factor, $\lambda_0 > 0$, while RCQ1 and RCQ2 are defined by negative values, $\lambda_0 < 0$. Our model is then tested using the latest observational data from high-z galaxy clusters and found to be consistent with current constraints.
