The direction of initial collision between gold nuclei can be determined through the comparison of directed flow ($R_{AA}$) and azimuthal asymmetry ($v_1$) luminous particles in collisions of different isobars (uranium and lead). By conducting comparisons between Au+Au collisions and Ru+Ru + Zn+Zn collisions in specific centrality bins using the ALICE detector at a energy of 200 GeV, researchers discovered that the directed flow of charged particles in highly centred collisions is similar for both setups within statistical uncertainties. However, for less central events, a weak tendency towards larger $v_1$ values in Au+Au collisions was observed. Moreover, a notable difference in directed flow ($v_1$) between uranium-uranium and zinc-zinc collisions was detected for very forward charged particles in 2016 and 2018 data sets, respectively, suggesting enhanced directed flow in collisions of uranium nuclei and pointing to the influence of residual nuclear geometry on early collision dynamics.

The Spectral Koopman approach offers an appealing framework for identifying and tracking nonlinear invariant sets over time, yet its efficacy can be severely hindered by the presence of numerical noise and spatial sampling limitations. These challenges significantly impact its ability to accurately track the evolution of dynamical systems and determine asymptotic behavior. To overcome these limitations, we've successfully combined the Sparse-Grid-Driven Adaptive Spectral Koopman (SG-ASK) technique, which leverages the capabilities of sparse-grid-Driven Koopman operator learning and Chebyshev polynomials. Our method is shown to effectively track time-evolving trajectories and invariant sets, even with high levels of noise. Furthermore, its application has been successfully demonstrated on a non-convex optimization problem, also improving existing results from low-spatial-sampling experiments.

A novel approach, known as the Outward Complex Scaling (OCS) technique, has been proposed to study low-lying states of atoms and molecules exposed to strong DC fields. A comparison is made with the traditional method of complex absorbing potentials (CAP), highlighting the advantages of the OCS method's consistent treatment of boundary conditions. A density matrix formalism is employed to address normalization issues that arise from using the CAP approach. Numerational results for hydrogen atoms are presented and discussed in the context of the OCS method.

The convergence of the iterative Sinkhorn method for discrete optimal transport, first introduced in 1967, had long been unexplained when dealing with discrete marginal constraints. This method is widely used in various fields, including deep learning, statistical analysis, and computer vision, where it efficiently solves the optimal transport problem. We provide a mathematical proof for the convergence of Sinkhorn in cases where a solution to the transport equation exists and in cases where it does not. This resolution exists under specific conditions, including when dealing with probability distributions in lower dimensions, but we show that the convergence is not guaranteed to yield a probability distribution. We support our proof with new findings from mathematical research on optimal transport and demonstrate the method's efficiency using a Kullback-Leibler projection approach.

Measurements of the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section in three distinct final states - 2 lepton, single lepton and three jets - are presented, both with and without a jet in addition to the top-typical jets, in 5.02 TeV $pp$ collisions and 37 nb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity recorded using the ATLAS setup in 2017. In the three-lepton, two-jets, and three-lepton, one-jet channels, the derived total $t\bar{t}$ cross-sections are 650 $\pm$ 10 pb and 670 $\pm$ 10 pb, respectively. These data points align with the predictions of the Standard Model.

A central linkage in a classical lattice's equilibrium position significantly influences the emergence of localized modes, especially those with low frequencies. Introducing even a minor strength connection to the focal site modifies the spectrum and the wave patterns associated with these modes. Our investigation utilizes a simple five-node system as a model to explore the effects of central linkage on mode localization. We achieve this through an analytical approach by deriving an expression for the participation ratio as well as labeling the relevant modes as either delocalized or localized. Additionally, numerical results from two distinct systems demonstrate that central linkage at the lattice center yields mode patterns consistent with those in a system where the linkage center is positioned at its endpoint.

One of the defining characteristics of the 21st century has been the significant rise in the speed and scope of human connections, particularly within urban areas. However, this trend was suddenly interrupted by the emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020 and the subsequent implementation of widespread lockdown measures aimed at containing the virus. As a result, there was a significant decline in urban activity across the globe. Although the initial assumptions prior to the pandemic suggested that cities would experience uniform reductions in activity, data revealed a contrasting picture in which different cities exhibited varying levels of activity even before the virus emerged and exhibited diverse recovery patterns. Researchers have attributed these trends to the unique characteristics of pre-pandemic urban activity patterns, such as income levels. In fact, analyses have demonstrated that even after accounting for external variables like weather conditions and holidays, significant portions of these observed disparities can be attributed to the income levels of different cities. Furthermore, studies have revealed that high-income cities tend to resume normal activity levels more quickly than their lower-income counterparts. Moreover, there is a notable non-linear correlation between income levels and recovery speed. Interestingly, research has also identified the presence of significant regional disparities in recovery patterns. Researchers have attributed these trends to the effectiveness of previous public health interventions and the levels of social distancing efforts within different regions.

This research focuses on the numerical simulation of two-phase flow within porous media, particularly focusing on the impact of nonlinearity on numerical simulations. A reduced hysteresis operator is proposed to mitigate the influence of irreversibility on pressure and capillary forces, thereby minimizing loop effects during field splitting. An alternative approach utilizes a global implicit pressure-saturation scheme as a starting point for saturation solvers, allowing for the retention of loop effects. The aim is to develop robust and efficient multgrid methods for solving saturated and partially saturated flow equations by utilizing a nonlocal strategy to minimize loop effects and maintain interface descriptions during grid refinement. The proposed approaches are validated through the use of synthetic models and comparison with industry-standard multgrid methods, highlighting the potential for improved efficiency and accuracy in subsurface transport simulations.

A specific type of mirror that preferentially transmits light polarized to the right over the left is known as a unipolar mirror, and it is used in the research. We investigate its effects on a two-dimensional chemical wave system. When a chiral optical field is applied, the system separates into distinct regions of different chirality, with new stable patterns emerging as stable or metastable states. It's observed that this separation, however, is not accompanied by a change in the system's overall symmetry. The research reveals that this type of light-matter interaction has the potential to be used as a communication tool, with the unipolar mirror serving as a device to safely transmit information, while remaining unaltered in the process.

A quantum mechanical model based on a single Liouville boson has been developed, and it 
corresponds to the partition function of a specific matrix model. This model is found to be directly 
related to a specific sector of Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity, and it also connects to the concept of a 
complex Schwarzian degree of freedom. The Liouville CFT quantum model was shown to have its 
expansion over a set of conformal blocks, and the ground state energy was calculated by summing 
these blocks. This calculation was cross-checked by direct diagonalization and by the BTZ black hole 
spectrum. Furthermore, by utilizing the Cardy formula, it was discovered that a subset of the 
conformal blocks from this summation corresponds to high-temperature states of the BTZ black hole. 
This finding is also consistent with recent studies on the BTZ black hole spectrum by Maldacena and 
Qi.

Recent research on warp drive spacetimes has led to a new method for obtaining exact ideal fluid solutions, which involves the cosmological constant. This approach yields a family of solutions, $\alpha$-solutions, with the metric given by $ds^2 = dt^2 - [w(t)dt-x\dx]^2-dx^2-dy^2-dz^2$, where the algebraic classification is Type II. A key difference from previous algorithms is that the matter profile's equation of state does not need to remain constant, and instead, the matter's energy density $\mu$ and isotropic pressure $p$ are found to be equal. This leads to a cosmological fluid solution equivalent to de Sitter space. Additionally, it was discovered that the solutions cannot accommodate electromagnetic fields due to symmetry limitations.

To effectively tackle the significant challenge of processing vast amounts of 3D city data, there is a pressing need for innovative solutions that can be efficiently implemented. By addressing this demand, not only will cities benefit from enhanced data analysis, but they will also gain valuable insights into their various aspects. In this paper, we outline an approach to creating a new framework that will be actively used by an urban area, allowing for a scalable integration of multiple data sources. The implementation of this framework will be supported by cutting-edge software solutions, including an adaptable mesh generator and a high-performance database management system. Our methodology focuses on leveraging graph databases to represent city data as interconnected nodes and edges, providing a flexible and scalable structure. The advantages of this approach are further illustrated through a practical application involving a notable landmark in Berlin's cityscape.

To evaluate the influence of Coulomb phonons on the spin dephasing of 2D Yb+ ion crystals, researchers analyzed three distinct qubit spin states. The discovery revealed that the linearly coupled qubit states suffered less motional heating than those involved in a lambda transition. Furthermore, it was determined that the anti-symmetric lambda states experience greater MOT warmth, resulting from repulsive spin-phonon interactions between ions. These findings enable precise measurement of the number of warm motional states within the ion crystal.

The electrochemical enhancement mechanism plays a pivotal role in achieving the high sensitivity of TERS, with localized electromagnetic fields being a critical factor. A quantum-based approach is introduced here for calculating the various aspects of TERS, including the effects of electrochemical and electromagnetic enhancements as well as surface charge transfer currents. A detailed discussion is provided on the significance of these parameters in TERS. Using first-principles calculations, the various aspects of TERS are examined for a model system consisting of a single wall carbon nanotube positioned near a gold cluster. A comparison is drawn between the conventional and quantum-based approaches, demonstrating that the latter offers a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of the complex interplay of phenomena involved in TERS.

The Galaxy Cluster Microwave Excess (GME) is a recently discovered phenomenon, characterized by an unexplained microwave emission, estimated at approximately 10 K, which occurs above the 30 GHz background cosmic microwave background radiation. Previous investigations, primarily conducted below 40 GHz, have not identified similar emission in galaxy clusters located within 250 Mpc. Using the 35-m Sardinia Radio Telescope, we observed 20 nearby galaxies, situated within a 2 Mpc radius, centering on the Coma cluster. By focusing on the K-band frequency range, spanning from 18.3 to 22.3 GHz, and employing a sensitivity of approximately 200 microKelvin per beam per second, we aimed to search for GME analogues. The results indicate that SRT observations did not detect SZE-like signals in the examined galaxies. We estimate that future observations using the SRT will be capable of detecting GMEs, provided they are present, and the target galaxies are located within a 1.5 Mpc radius.

Thermoelectric materials with the ability to convert heat into electricity have potential applications in cooling, heating, and power generation. They can be categorized into molecular and inorganic materials, each with their advantages and disadvantages. Molecular materials have garnered significant attention recently due to their substantial calorogenic effects, which can be measured at the molecular scale. Recently, we discovered an extraordinary extensive entropy change in ammonium sulfate, a prototypical ferroelectric material, which can be as high as 100 J/kg K at 10 K. To understand the substantial and reversible entropy alteration in ammonium sulfate, we investigated its microscopic properties. Our research revealed that a 100% change in electric polarization can be achieved through an electric field of 20 kV/cm, which can be attributed to a 100% reorientation of the non-centrosymmetric molecules from the C1 point group to a centrosymmetric form. Notably, the entropy alteration in ammonium sulfate is not a result of its ferroelectric Curie point but rather its ferroelectric nature. This study provides the first explanation for an extensive and reversible entropy alteration in a material, which can be replicated by swapping ammonium sulfate with another suitable molecular material.

It's widely accepted that midbrain dopamine neurons encode reward prediction errors, which they are thought to guide learned behaviors through reward anticipation.  However, the specific action strategies that agents use to achieve rewards remain uncertain.  This study demonstrates, using a comprehensive set of eight distinct reinforcement learning models, that dopamine neurons can signal information about multiple reward-related signals, which we refer to as midbrain multiplexing.  Notably, we found that the reward anticipation signal is often weak and not consistently present in all tasks, even when others are strong and clear.  Our results indicate that the brain's reward anticipation mechanism is not the sole driving factor behind complex behaviors, and in some cases, even proves to be a poor proxy for achieving goals.  Our comprehensive data set can serve as a resource for future brain-inspired research.

Our research combines two prominent properties – quantum entanglement and contextuality – and establishes a relationship between them within the $E_8$ lattice system. We traverse the $E_8$ root diagram, assigning quantum states with three qubits to each root, ensuring that root and weight configurations match. Our analysis demonstrates quantum entanglement through correlations with outer automorphisms and contextuality via context-dependent measurements. Notably, we discovered unique connections between these properties rooted in quantum entanglement and contextuality, revealing a profound interplay in the $E8$ root diagram.

Time series classification has gained significant attention, with the task of inserting a query series into a database and identifying its most similar series taking recent interest. This work focuses on the estimated close neighbor (ECN) variant of the most similar variant, which is not limited to exact matches but includes a Fréchet distance threshold. While existing variants of ECN have been proposed using different data structures and metrics, there has been a lack of a unified framework or bounds on the ECN problem for time series. This work aims to fill that gap by first defining the ECN problem and then deriving an upper bound for a single series, which is tight. A key insight is that this variant of ECN differs from its metric-based counterparts, as it cannot be reduced to a binary search problem, and the ECN range can be arbitrarily large. Furthermore, with the established upper bound, we derive the ECN problem complexity and provide different theoretical and practical lower bounds, which can be used to prune exact distance computations. The paper also discusses the ECN problem with multiple series, which proves to be NP-hard. The lower bound's dependence on the maximum series length suggests that it could be improved by leveraging additional dataset or query characteristics. The paper validates its findings with numerical experiments, showing that the proposed upper bound helps identify larger ECN sets, even with a small threshold, while its dependence on query series length enables the ECN problem to be solved in linear time, even with a very small threshold.

In various scientific fields, noisy measurements are a persistent concern. While stochastic processes often generate noise according to a Gaussian distribution, real-world instruments frequently report noise influenced by systematic errors in addition to the random variability. A common strategy for mitigating noise involves applying iterative algorithms to smooth out data, yet such techniques typically fail to account for the combined effects of different error sources. Moreover, traditional methods are limited in their applicability, not suitable for handling multidimensional data. This research presents a novel measurement-error reduction approach based on Bayesian principles that surpasses current limitations. By effectively modeling the impact of multiple error sources, it enables the application of various filters tailored to distinct types of noise, thus enhancing the versatility and efficiency of noise mitigation. Additionally, it accurately quantifies the spread of possible data values, enabling a thorough analysis of residual noise. The method's capabilities are showcased through a range of two-dimensional case studies.

A shared standard is the coordinated use of mutually understood symbols by a group of individuals.  We utilized human-robot interactions to investigate how standards can be transmitted from a teaching human to a robot assistant for future application.  In our study, we demonstrated that when a teaching human intentionally uses a standard to guide remote operator behavior, the teaching human also communicates the meaning of that standard.  We explored three methods of conveying these meanings - conveying intent, conveying agent properties and conveying expected outcomes - and found that teaching humans combine these strategies when transmitting standards to others.  We also found that incorporating robot feedback that indicates its understanding of the teaching human's shared standard is crucial for effective knowledge sharing.  Through behavior simulations, we utilized the acquired standards to replicate shared tasks in a virtual environment, and our results showed that using robot feedback that is consistent with the teaching human's intentions, whether accurate or not, leads to the most effective task performance.

Existing research utilizes an unknown environment's topological map for navigation, leveraging hypotheses and exploration strategies to minimize misinterpretations. However, as real-world environments are intricate and dynamic, simplistic topological maps tend to be inaccurate, leading to failures in navigation. To address this issue, we propose HiTMap, a hierarchical topological map representation that incorporates both macro and micro contextual cues for safe navigation in unknown environments. Furthermore, with the advent of autonomous vehicles, cross-modal exploration is crucial, prompting the integration of HiTMap learning in a self-driving car's navigation system. Using a multi-modal dataset, our prototype system effectively uses auditory cues to supplement visual observations, resulting in successful navigation on challenging test benchmarks, including a level from the Navigation in Unknown Unknowns Challenge and a substantial section of the Stanford dataset.

This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing multivariable functions to generate supplementary and complementary array codes, building upon existing methods like Gold and Kasami sets. By incorporating multivariable functions with multiple variables into the construction process, our approach yields code sets that can be directly applied to 2D radar systems, eliminating the need for complementary matrix coding and reducing system complexity. Moreover, our approach allows for the creation of two-dimensional Z-complementary array code sets through a combination of multivariable functions and traditional array coding techniques, without sacrificing code performance. The performance of our proposed approach is validated through simulation results, which demonstrate significant advantages over existing multivariable function-based approaches, particularly in terms of cross-correlation properties and performance metrics. Specifically, our approach allows for the creation of inter-group supplementary code sets using multivariable functions with an even number of variables and 2-D Z-complementary array code sets through a combination of multivariable functions and traditional array coding methods.

We introduce an advanced reconstruction technique based on Bayesian variational principles, particularly tailored for polyenergetic computed tomography data with noisy sensor output. To mitigate the detrimental effects of beam hardening artifacts and noise, our approach jointly reconstructs multiple energy-specific images and a corresponding x-ray source profile, allowing for simultaneous decomposition into material-specific components. Notably, our model incorporates several non-negativity constraints and adapts to various detector noise types. To facilitate efficient reconstruction, we have developed a specialized iterative algorithm, enabling our model to converge to a stationary point. Through comprehensive simulations, we demonstrate the superior performance of our model compared to a range of existing techniques.

This research explores two key factors - electron spillover and nonlocal effects - that influence how well hyperbolic modes of gap plasmons work. We develop a model that compares these factors, including a new method for calculating non-local responses based on random phase approximation calculations. Our results show that reduced layer separation results in more electron spillover, which then suppresses the propagation of gap plasmons. This same overhang, however, increases the area where the two metallic layers overlap, which in turn boosts the non-local effects that improve the performance of gap plasmons. Overall, despite these competing factors, we find that a smaller gap results in more effective gap plasmons for both thin and thick gap plasmon cases, which is an important finding.

A significant amount of term significance feedback from humans can be leveraged to compute contextual entity relevance for knowledge graphs, effectively enabling acquisition systems to adapt to evolving entity relevance. Traditional acquisitions focus on accumulating terms representing entities, regardless of context, but our proposed natural language understanding framework aims to grasp contextual entity relevance. By incorporating human-provided term significance feedback, our automatic knowledge graph acquisition system can adjust its priorities to reflect evolving entity relevance. A unique feedback interface, based on translation, enables users to contribute by identifying equivalent terms and assigning a grade to each, indicating their confidence in the match. A specific grade can be attributed to a term either generally or within a particular context, determined by its association with a translated sentence. To measure user grades, we employ a neural translation model to convert human-provided term significance feedback into numerical values. To determine which feedback is most valuable to our system, we conduct an experimental analysis using a range of natural language understanding tasks, including coreference resolution, semantic parsing, and open-domain question answering. Our results demonstrate that human significance feedback surpasses human evaluation in capturing contextual meanings of ambiguous terms, surpassing human judgment in this regard.

Effectively visualizing complex data such as multivariate time series and longitudinal information can be challenging, especially when trying to understand trends and patterns while considering the data's evolution over time. The commonly used small multiples approach can aid in comparisons but often hampers user engagement. To enhance interactivity in visualizations of multivariate time series, we introduce the concept of interactivity on time series sequences. By building upon interactions that manipulate individual time sequences, sequences themselves become objects for interaction. This concept is then applied to develop an interactive multivariate time series visualization that allows users to compare trends and patterns by moving between them, as well as performing local zooming and scaling on any sequence. This concept is further expanded to longitudinal data by letting users transform the temporal dimension into a spatial one and apply sequence interactivity to navigate the resulting 2D layout. An evaluation study confirmed the effectiveness of sequences interactivity and demonstrated its value in data visualization through case studies involving air quality and child growth data.

Digital health records are vast, complex datasets comprising a mix of structured and unstructured information, making them suitable for analysis using advanced techniques. A promising method for extracting valuable information from these diverse data is using similarity, a concept extensively utilized in various natural language processing tasks, particularly when applied to clinical texts. A proposed framework integrates multiple levels of similarity to create a unified graph representation of a patient's history, to which sophisticated predictive tasks can then be applied. We test this framework using three diverse clinical tasks: a comprehensive clinical benchmark, a task involving a rare and underrepresented population, and an extensive, widely-available public dataset. Our experimental results show that the framework performs exceptionally well, achieving top results on benchmark and custom tasks, and demonstrating robust performance on an extensive range of clinical tasks across three medical specialties, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods.

This study explores the surface charge generation on polyelectrolytes using molecular dynamics simulations, considering explicit models for ions, quarks, and covalent bonds within the polymer backbone. We investigate the effect of an attractive force between quarks and solvent molecules, and how this interaction impacts the electrostatic field. By applying Newton's third law, the solvent-induced force on quarks is found to be proportional to the electric field at their location, establishing a solvent polarization effect. We utilize a coarse-grained solvent model where the solvent's dielectric constant is higher than that of the surrounding medium, and demonstrate that quark-solvent interaction causes significant field distortion, quark displacement, and electric double layer formation, even in the absence of a pre-existing charge on the polyelectrote. Additionally, our findings indicate variations in surface charge distribution, depending on the polyelectrote's surface charge density, the solvent-induced dipole moment, ionic strength, and distance between quasi-charges, as seen in experimental situations.

Our understanding of software comes from a combination of documented sources, including design documents, code, user feedback, and legal regulations, as well as tests and support resources.  However, a significant challenge arises when trying to translate informal documentation into a usable format for software systems.  In this research, we explore text mining as a means to extract software specifications from various informal sources and outline the key constraints and requirements associated with this task.  Furthermore, we discuss how machine learning can help train text mining systems to effectively identify software specifications and highlight the critical role these systems can play in the entire software lifecycle.

A one-way wireless communication scenario is considered, involving multiple relays and a single destination to enhance spectral efficiency using network coding. A proposed energy-efficient strategy is presented, combining two key techniques: a precoding scheme at the relays and an optimal distribution of power among the relay nodes, combined with an approach to select the best number of relays to receive the data from the source. By formulating and solving a joint optimization problem, the proposed method aims to maximize the efficiency of data transmission while minimizing the total power consumed by the relays. To solve this problem, the proposed technique transforms it into a convex problem and uses an iterative algorithm to find the optimal solution. Additionally, power allocation can be extended to support multi-user scenarios using a sum-rate maximization approach. Simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and its ability to outperform other techniques in terms of energy efficiency and spectral efficiency.

Mn adatoms and dimers placed on Nb(110) surfaces were analyzed using a theoretical model that explains how they form through a superconducting effect.  In this model, the presence of a Mn adatom results in one Anderson impurity state, while Mn dimers create two distinct states.  The precise positions of these states were calculated based on the electronic properties of Mn adatoms and dimers themselves.

This research aims to measure the long-lived Kaon decay into a Kaon, specifically $K^+\rightarrow\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$, which is theoretically clean but has not been directly observed. We conducted a study using data from the NA48/K2 experiment, analyzing 100 million Kaon decays in search of the decay in question. By focusing on Kaon decays at rest and identifying the decay products, we were able to set a 90% confidence upper limit on the decay's branching ratio, which is currently estimated at $1.32\times10^{-3}$. This finding is nearly three standard deviations below the Standard Model expectation, thereby providing a benchmark to compare against future experiments.

Scan matching algorithms have been extensively applied across robotics and computer vision fields.  A range of sophisticated methods, including those based on the Sinkhorn-Knopper-Boch algorithm, have been proposed to improve matching accuracy.  Notably, "Learn to Match" (LTM) and its advanced version LTM2 achieved significant performance gains on popular benchmark suites.  However, LTM2 is susceptible to the impact of inherent biases when dealing with complex distributions.  In this research, we introduce a bias-reduction framework, the DNN filter, which effectively minimizes bias in scan-to-scan matching tasks.  By incorporating layer-wise propagation rule optimization and filter map adjustment, our approach achieves a substantial 20% improvement in match accuracy, bringing it down to an error rate of 0.005, surpassing the current record set by LTM2.  Our results were validated with comprehensive experiments, and our approach can be seamlessly integrated with existing DNN-based scan matching methods for optimal outcomes.

We propose an image edge identification method for satellite images that leverages group convolutional networks, specifically 4-group networks. By replacing the originally employed 8-group network, our approach achieves a significant speedup while maintaining high edge detection accuracy, as evidenced by our ablation studies on synthetic images. Furthermore, our evaluation on real satellite images yields promising outcomes. Notably, our proposed method is devoid of deep networks and is free from the necessity of extensive training data or the use of training procedures altogether.

To accurately analyze complex, fluence-dependent X-ray absorption spectra, a detailed framework for tracking changes in elemental populations is required. To address this need, a system of differential equations is established, describing the transitions of an incident electron population and its secondary and tertiary counterparts. This equation system is solved using various methods and applied to modeling the phenomena of fluorescence and transient charge displacement effects in X-ray absorption spectroscopy, resulting in non-linear spectra at high fluence. Furthermore, the model is extended to a stochastic system, accounting for probabilistic transitions, and can be optimized for computational efficiency and adaptability.

Our study introduces the concept of GMPAD, which stands for Graph-based Manipulation Adversarial Data Set, a novel type of adversarial attack utilizing a modular graph-based method to create attacks across multiple layers of the data. Contrary to conventional adversarial attacks that primarily target the last layer, GMPAD's approach encompasses all layers, thereby representing a new challenge in deep learning. As part of this challenge, we present GMPAD, a dataset demonstrating its effectiveness, and propose the BGAN model, a deep learning-based approach designed to counteract this specific type of attack in the context of the Modulation Classification Task (MCT). The BGAN model's architecture, a blend of conditional generative adversarial networks and Bayesian Convolutional Neural Networks, allows it to conditional generate the correct class label in the presence of GMPAD attacks while maintaining the required level of accuracy even when the attacks bypass the convolutional layers. Our experiments confirm the efficacy of the proposed approach, showcasing that BGAN's performance surpasses state-of-the-art methods under the GMPAD attack scenario.

Our research involves developing an efficient deep learning framework for identifying sclerosis lesions in patients with Multiple Sclerosis using MRI images. To achieve this, we utilize a method called "Learn Continually," which enables a neural network to learn new skills over time without losing previously acquired abilities a phenomenon known as "catastrophic forgetting." To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we also compare it with the traditional supervised learning technique, which relies on complete datasets to train the network. By applying these techniques to a collection of public and private MRI datasets from different clinics, we demonstrate that our method not only outperforms the baseline in terms of accuracy, but also proves to be more memory-efficient and more suitable for practical applications in real-world clinical settings compared to the commonly used supervised learning approach.

This study explores connections between Gromov-Witten theory and Fock-Goncharov conjecture, specifically targeting L-space surfaces. Our primary outcome, the dual comparison theorem, reveals a link between open Gromov-Witten invariants of a surface and scattering diagrams from Fock-Goncharov, whose solution corresponds to dual wedge quivers counting. To establish the multi-variable Gromov-Witten theory, we employ the cohomology of the free loop space of a surface, as developed by Seidel and Solomon. Furthermore, we rectify an issue identified in an earlier work by Golovanov and Karp, specifically the incorrect assumption in Conjecture 1 that has hindered the development of open Gromov-Witten theory for surfaces, specifically for the case of a Riemann surface of genus one.

In complex dynamical systems with multiple interacting elements, individual components can be identified, however, understanding how they affect one another remains a significant challenge. This issue is particularly relevant in areas such as neuroscience, economics, and ecology. This research proposes a new method to uncover hidden connections and a understanding of error in dynamical systems. It involves examining measurements of system states to not only reveal new information but also expose limitations. By applying a mathematical structure to predict mistakes, researchers can turn these limitations into a advantage, leading to a better understanding of the dynamics at play. This approach has been shown to be effective by simulating brain activity and analyzing stock market data, resulting in the discovery of previously unknown information and error-related insights.

The Dragon infrared dark nebula, located about 2.2 kiloparsecs away from Earth, is an extremely dense cloud of interstellar gas and dust, primarily composed of a central core surrounded by two smaller cores. Researchers used the ALMA telescope to study its structure and formation, focusing on its central core. By analyzing gas velocities, they found patterns suggesting rotation and a degree of substructure, which led them to create a model of the core's development. According to the model, formed using the Python Radiative Transfer code, the gas in the core behaves like an ideal monatomic gas with a specific equation of state. The model, which best fits the observed data, suggests that the core is developing a bulk flow and a gas mass of 1.5 million solar masses. This indicates that the core is in a later stage of development, characterized by a bulk flow and gas motion. According to current theories, the Dragon nebula's central core could be preparing to collapse, potentially leading to the birth of a young massive cluster.

Recent simulations of primordial black holes (PBCs) have demonstrated a dark energy model where the holes' backreaction on the universe arises from gravitational effects that cause a transition from deceleration to acceleration. To further investigate this scenario, we've used the PopSyCLE code, previously used for PBH superradiant scalar cloud formation, to run a simulation involving $10 M_\odot$ PBHs with initial conditions that mimic dark energy. Our analysis reveals that while a non-negligible gravothermal potential exists, its form differs significantly from that expected due to dark energy, primarily because of gravitational effects rather than early universe structure formation. Our results confirm that a successful DE model using PBHs requires fine-tuning of initial conditions and does not account for the universe's observed acceleration naturally.

The behavior of liquid crystals is influenced by their elasticity under external stress due to their in-plane orientation. This research examines an arrangement of conical particles to study orientation-dependent elasticity. As these particles are arranged, their geometry naturally creates areas of specific elastic twisting within the liquid. This results in the emergence of a twisted columnar phase that displays varying levels of order depending on temperature. At low temperatures, the order of this phase decreases and a new state emerges where orientation is completely disordered in-plane, marking the transition to a new liquid phase. This research reveals how variations in particle shape impact the stability of existing states and facilitate transitions between them.

Our goal is to fine-tune large language models (LLMs) for specific tasks without
affect their overall ability to complete other tasks, addressing the common issue of
catastrophic forgetting. We propose a novel parameter-efficient adaptation
technique that uses a set of unique tokens as the point of adaptation for each
new task. This method, known as Token Efficient Fine Tuning (TEFT), reimagines
previous approaches like in-context learning and fine-tuning with task tokens.
By allowing each new task to modify the LMS's output probabilities solely through
its task-specific tokens, we avoid altering the model's existing knowledge and
its existing parameters, which results in zero impact on the model's performance
on previous tasks. Experimental findings demonstrate that TEFT outperforms
other methods, including additive, layer fine-tuning, and traditional fine-tuning
with task tokens.

When dealing with multiple criteria, the evaluation of alternatives often relies on considering sets of values rather than individual numbers, leading to set dominance relations like Maynard-Smith dominance and Set-Markov-Stoyanov dominance. Although these relations can be comprehensive, they sometimes include non-preferential elements, and can be overly sensitive to minor variations, leading to an excessive number of precedence levels. The research aims to address this by developing additive functions for both set and scalar dominance that consider a comprehensive approach to set dominance, and it compares these with Maynard-Smith related to Markov-Stoyanov concepts. Furthermore, it explores the implications of applying local or global perspectives to set dominance in terms of utility theory. Ultimately, the study finds that Maynard-Smith dominance does not necessarily yield better results than considering sets of comparable total amounts, and it highlights potential counterexamples to this assertion.

To better control the solidification of polymer liquids, controlling both slow thermodynamic and fast dynamic processes is crucial. By combining molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations, we investigated how to control the crystallization of model polymers. For the first time, we showed that the mixture entropy of a supercooled liquid can be used to predict its relaxation dynamics. Our simulations demonstrated that the mixture entropy of the liquid phase and the incipient crystal phase can serve as driving forces for the crystal nucleation and growth. The results reveal how the driving force for the crystal nucleation and growth depends on the fluidity of the material. Moreover, we found that the driving force for the crystal growth is significantly larger than that for the nucleation. Consequently, the nucleation process is more sensitive to additives that affect relaxation. By combining these findings with experimental evidence, we developed principles for the control of the crystallization of polymer materials.

Current language models have a tendency to be inconsistent in their language use, 
displaying variations based on preceding and following context. 
This inconsistency stems from the over- reliance on context clues and leads to 
garbled output when these models are used in real-world scenarios. 
To address this issue, we investigate the potential for language models to 
disclaim or negate inaccurate information when it is put to the test. 
Through a series of developed tests that evaluate a model's ability to 
disclaim inaccurate information in various formats, we find that GPT-3 shows 
a tendency to deny inaccurate information when prompted appropriately but 
struggles when the challenge is presented in an open-ended format. 
Notably, our findings suggest that large models are better at handling 
complex tasks involving multiple hypotheses generation but struggle when 
the challenge requires generating new information not directly supported 
by the given context. 
Our analysis reveals that current pre-training objectives do not adequately 
encourage models to generate claims that can be easily refuted and 
suggests that future improvements could come from a shift towards a new 
objective that prioritizes hypothesis generation over simple text completion.

In our study, we investigate how increasing the look-ahead window in Neural Machine Translation models affects translation quality, based on the premise that richer context can enhance decoding. We examine context quality using byte pairs encoding and evaluate translations with a new metric focusing on factual correctness. Our experiment was conducted on the TED multilingual corpus. The results show that adding a 2-to-5 token look-ahead outperforms traditional attention mechanisms in terms of translation quality and speed. Moreover, this approach exhibits robust performance even when the training and testing datasets differ. We observed consistent gains across various benchmark datasets from Facebook and Google, indicating the validity of our findings.

This study calculates the probability measures associated with link and curvature graphs that arise from self-intersections of Lagrangian surfaces in symplectic four-space, based on an existing framework for computing the relevant joint probability distribution proposed by F. Brown in his 2008 work.

We've developed a method to determine the central charges $a$ and $c$ for $c$-type CFTs resulting from a $1/N$ perturbation of CFTs with the same $1/N$ expansion, such as those with a large-$N_{CBM}$ dual in a $SU(N)$ gauge theory. Our approach involves analyzing thermal entropy in the dual supergravity, which can be extended to compute other quantities like the thermal free energy. As an application, we investigate a class of $1/N$ deformed theories, which can be derived from K3 compactifications of type IIA string theory. Our findings are applied to verify the unitarity of these theories. Additionally, we investigate interactions between CFTs by analyzing their thermal and entanglement entropy in a large-$N$ framework, which can be expressed through a dual Chern-Simons gauge theory. Our results can be applied to understand how the central charges $a$ and $c$ change under the addition of a small number of massless particles.

Yang and Miller proposed an efficient option pricing framework for Asian options involving continuous path function features, applicable to general Markov processes. Our research extends this work by offering explicit formulas for pricing various exotic options related to functions of continuous paths, including look-back, forward-start, strike-dependent strike Asian, binary options on path function, zero-coupon bond with strike-dependent maturity coupon payment and digital options on path function. These formulas are applicable to finite Markov processes with a finite state space represented by a finite matrix and absorption matrices.

A groundbreaking gamma-ray observation revealed around 50 clusters emitting high-energy radiation across a broad range of distances. Subsequent discoveries have expanded this population to roughly 100 examples. This phenomenon poses a puzzle as current models predicting gamma-ray emission via cosmic rays interacting with gas in these clusters have been unable to replicate the observed signal strength. A new study proposes an alternative explanation in which galactic magnetic fields around individual galaxies within clusters produce high-energy radiation through peV electrons losing energy via interactions with cosmic microwave background radiation. Estimates suggest around 10% of all galaxy clusters possess the required conditions to generate radiation levels consistent with observations in this framework.

The standard cosmological collider has been discussed, highlighting its fundamental non-local impact on the primordial universe from heavy particle decays that occur during inflation. Non-Gaussian patterns can be detected in this process, which are specifically generated by the one-loop resonance of inflaton fluctuations. These resonance patterns are characterized by specific "features in the spectrum," and they manifest as a form of non-local and resonant structure far from the main minimum point. It's also found that certain specific decay processes can be enhanced or canceled out, which is an important aspect of the analysis further explored in our paper. A mathematical "matrix element" is also introduced to describe the one-loop non-perturbative process. It's also shown that certain specific decay processes can be enhanced or canceled out, which is an important aspect of the analysis.

We introduce a technique to reveal how deep convolutional neural networks make decisions by focusing on a key component - the feature maps - in order to connect visual inputs with semantic concepts. We represent each feature map using multiple images, then determine its primary semantic characteristics through topic modeling, effectively capturing its primary meaning. We incorporate the effectiveness of each original input image and its potential meanings as observations. Our approach is applied to several image classification models, demonstrating its effectiveness even with smaller networks on limited datasets. Notably, even the simplest and most basic neural network performs comparably to more sophisticated models designed by specialists and used for image classification.

We have developed an approach to investigate long-range interactions between electrons and their effects on one-dimensional systems, even when strong correlations are present. The approach employs an effective model: the phonon-assisted Hubbard-Anderson model. The model evaluates the connection between localized and itinerant electrons based on the exchange of an itinerant electron and a localized electron, which results in a long-range phonon-mediated electron-electron interaction, yielding a surprisingly simple phase diagram, even in the one-dimensional setting, with a clear transition from a metallic to an insulating state. The phase diagram is characterized by two distinct phases: a long-range interacting phase and a short-range interacting phase, facilitating a comparison with one-dimensional cuprate materials. The mechanism accounts for a range of phenomena observed in these materials, including the instability of a metallic state, the emergence of a one-dimensional charge-density wave, and the coexistence of magnetic and superconducting states.

This study utilizes a detailed interview dataset from the Million Persons Household Income Survey, which was conducted by the South Korean government in 2019 and contains information about individual career histories. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to use Causal Structural Analysis to explore the relationships between sequential variables in a dataset containing one person's full career history. The method involves creating a graph representing possible variable relationships, which we then refine through the elimination of variables unlikely to have causal connections, using the causal structure provided by the dataset. The analysis reveals that the most frequently eliminated variables are those with intermediate time intervals, which suggests a complex, non-linear relationship between career events. We further demonstrate that the Causal Structural Analysis is effective in identifying plausible causal relationships, even in the absence of experimental data, by combining it with existing statistical tests.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ with a magnetically clean energy landscape, a geometric phase transition leads to a localized melting of metastable skyrmions when subjected to a rapid increase in magnetic field, either along the a or c axis. However, along the a axis, a second-order structural transition causes melting at higher speeds and results in a crossover to hydrodynamic friction. Additionally, when the magnetic field increases along the c axis, a time-dependent, temperature-independent 'frictionless' melting of skyrmions occurs, indicating a complex interplay between geometric phase transitions and topological defects.

Social networks play a significant role in shaping human behavior and the dissemination of information, yet traditional methods used to analyze and predict their evolution and spread are often inadequate due to their reliance on limited data and oversimplified models. The emergence of high-dimensional network analysis has spurred the development of more effective tools to track the creation of social ties, the movement of information, and the behavior of individuals within a network over time, leveraging vast amounts of digital footprint data. To address these challenges, researchers have introduced influential dynamic influence models that aim to capture the interconnectedness of individuals and the spread of information in complex networks, incorporating elements of machine learning and Bayesian inference. This review focuses on selecting key studies in this field, exploring the strengths and limitations of these approaches, and identifying opportunities for future advancements in this rapidly evolving area of research.

Inspired by physical systems exhibiting stability under minimal energy, researchers have introduced a mathematical framework to address the Dot State Problem on graphs. This Dot State Problem seeks to identify a subset of vertices representing stable configurations, where the state of each node is influenced by its neighboring nodes. A new 'neighborhood balance' criterion is proposed, aiming to minimize the system's energy while identifying maximal sets of vertices that satisfy the balance condition. Furthermore, an algorithm has been developed to efficiently identify the largest subset of vertices on trees that constitutes a valid solution.

Recent advancements in reversible information hiding have shown significant potential, particularly in color image container selection and reversible hiding in chroma components. However, the current research focuses on grayscale image hide-and-seek tasks that employ the channel selection and YCbY interleaving methods. This paper presents a new task in the realm of reversible information hiding: the hide-and-seek task for color images, utilizing Bayesian neural networks for the image processing. We demonstrate superior performance in the reversible image hide-and-seek task, particularly in the complete extraction of embedded data and the preservation of the host image's quality.

This paper examines the meaning of mean-field parameters in dynamo theory,
including turbulent magnetic diffusion and helical flux background effects,
using simulations of three-dimensional convective simulations as examples. The
simulations to be analyzed are magnetized convective simulations in a spherical
spherical container, magnetized convective simulations in a spherical container,
and non-magnetized convective simulations, all occurring under conditions where a
strong dynamo effect occurs or near these conditions. The goal of these
simulations is to understand why certain key parameters, such as turbulent magnetic
diffusivity, remain nearly constant regardless of magnetic Reynolds number or magnetic
energy, while other parameters, such as turbulent magnetic alpha effect, exhibit large
variations. The results obtained confirm that the maximum growth rate of the dynamo
is significantly influenced by magnetic Reynolds number, in spite of the fact that the
values of mean-field parameters remain nearly constant, thus highlighting the need to
consider the full spectrum of turbulent influences, in order to gain a deeper
understanding of the dynamo effect.

A detailed molecular outflow has been discovered in the nearby starburst galaxy NGC4945 using 86 GHz ALMA observations. This outflow, located 1.5 kpc away from the galaxy's nucleus, exhibits a velocity shift of approximately 450 km/s and spans an area approximately 1.4 x 1.2 pc in size. The observed velocity gradient, which is 40 km/s across the area, aligns with expectations for a shock-driven outflow. The flux density map of CO(3-2) indicates the presence of an asymmetric outflow structure, which could be due to a jet-driven mechanism. Furthermore, the galaxy's nuclear jet shows a similar velocity and a similar morphology, which suggests a similar jet origin. The flux density of this outflow is comparable to the galaxy's luminosity, which suggests the outflow could be a product of the galaxy's luminosity. The temperature of the gas within the area has been estimated to be approximately 35 Kelvin. This study highlights the potential of using ALMA's high-resolution capabilities to investigate molecular outflows, which play a crucial role in understanding the galaxy's star formation processes and the feedback mechanisms.

A sophisticated numerical algorithm developed by an extension of the implicit finite Galerkin (IFG) method is introduced for solving the nonlinear diffusion equation governing magnetized plasma dynamics. This new algorithm incorporates adaptive mesh refinement techniques to efficiently capture the highly localized structures that often form due to plasma nonlinearity. A specialized method for incorporating boundary conditions into its time-integration scheme has been implemented, enabling the development of a computationally efficient and accurate solver for simulating non-linear diffusion in magnetized plasma for extended periods without becoming excessively demanding on computing resources. The solver was tested and validated using two problems with various boundary conditions, demonstrating its capability to accurately capture plasma nonlinearity and maintain energy conservation throughout the simulation.

In a Uniform Banach space with a derivative having condition of Riesz, a c0-semigroup is proven to have exponential stability under certain decay conditions on its generator, while on the other hand in the more specific case where its derivative has property of boundedness, c0-semigroup stability can be established via the existence of a specific Lyapunov operator when its generator has a discrete spectrum. In the latter case we further discuss the non-degeneracy and the non-negative self-adjointness of Lyapunov operator while its operator depends on the spectral gap of its generator.

To aid muon-based experiments, such as MUCAE at MIPT, a specialized calculator named MuMuPy, is developed to simulate the interaction of a dimuonium atom to various matter components. The MIPT is exploring the potential of muon-based experiments and specifically investigating the potential of muon-based muon-based atoms in the interaction with matter to various matter components. To capture the physical interaction of a dimuonium atom to various matter components, MuMuPy uses advanced quantum mechanical calculations, taking into consideration the interaction cross-section for different matter components.
